It feels like a heavy pressure over his sternum. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes per day for 40 years and was diagnosed with hyperlipidaemia 20 years ago. An initial ECG is performed. ECG ST elevation in V3 and V4 Despite resuscitative measures the patient dies. At autopsy, an haematoxylin and eosin stained section of the left anterior descending artery shows atheroma formation. Which of the following best describes the last step involved in the pathogenesis of his autopsy finding?
options: Appearance of foam cells in the intima
Smooth muscle migration from tunica media
explanation:
Smooth muscle migration from tunica media
Smooth muscle proliferation and migration from the tunica media into the intima is the last step in the formation of an atheroma.

Thickening of the tunica intima
Thickening of the tunica intima. Histologically, this is mainly composed of proteoglycan rich extracellular matrix and acellular lipid pools.

Development of fatty streaks
Fatty streaks are minimal lipid depositions on the luminal surface which are not necessarily a part of the atheroma. They can be seen in normal individuals also and begin as early as in the twenties.

Infiltration by macrophages & T-lymphocytes
As the pathological process evolves, we start seeing the early stages of fibroatheroma which is characterized primarily by infiltration of macrophages & T-lymphocytes, with the formation of a well-demarcated lipid-rich necrotic core.

Appearance of foam cells in the intima
The appearance of foam cells occur relatively early in the disease process and play a major role in the pathogenesis of atheroma formation.

stem: A 2-year-old boy presents to the paediatric clinic with developmental delay, coarse facial features, and hepatosplenomegaly. His parents report that he was developing normally until around 12 months of age when they noticed he began losing previously acquired skills. Investigations reveal cloudy corneas and skeletal abnormalities on X-ray. A skin biopsy is performed for fibroblast culture. Which cellular process is most likely defective in this patient?
explanation:
Golgi apparatus mannose-6-phosphate tagging
Golgi adds mannose-6-phosphate to proteins for trafficking to lysosomes. This patient presents with classic features of a lysosomal storage disorder, specifically mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS). The constellation of developmental regression, coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, corneal clouding, and skeletal abnormalities is highly suggestive of this diagnosis. Lysosomal storage disorders occur when there is a deficiency of specific lysosomal enzymes needed to break down various substrates, leading to their accumulation in tissues. The Golgi apparatus plays a crucial role in targeting newly synthesized lysosomal enzymes to lysosomes through mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tagging. This process involves the addition of M6P residues to specific N-linked oligosaccharides on lysosomal enzymes in the Golgi. These M6P tags are then recognized by mannose-6-phosphate receptors, which facilitate the transport of these enzymes from the Golgi to lysosomes. Defects in this tagging system can lead to misrouting of lysosomal enzymes, resulting in their secretion outside the cell rather than delivery to lysosomes. This causes a functional deficiency of lysosomal enzymes despite normal production, leading to the clinical manifestations of lysosomal storage disorders. I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II) is a specific example where this M6P tagging mechanism is defective.

Endoplasmic reticulum protein folding
Endoplasmic reticulum protein folding defects typically manifest as ER stress syndromes. While protein misfolding can contribute to some storage disorders, the clinical picture described is more consistent with defective trafficking of properly folded lysosomal enzymes rather than primary protein folding issues. ER protein folding disorders often present with different clinical features such as congenital disorders of glycosylation.

Mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation
Mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation defects typically present with features of energy deficiency such as muscle weakness, seizures, stroke-like episodes, and lactic acidosis. The progressive neurodevelopmental deterioration with multisystem involvement described in this case is more consistent with a lysosomal storage disorder rather than a primary mitochondrial disorder.

Peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation
Peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation defects, such as those seen in Zellweger syndrome, typically present with hypotonia, seizures, characteristic facial features, and liver dysfunction. While there is some overlap with the presented symptoms, peroxisomal disorders typically don't cause the corneal clouding and specific skeletal changes described in this case.

Proteasomal protein degradation
Proteasomal protein degradation abnormalities are associated with various disorders including neurodegenerative conditions and some forms of cancer. However, the constellation of symptoms described in this case, particularly the coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, and corneal clouding, is much more consistent with a lysosomal storage disorder than a primary proteasomal dysfunction.

stem: A 6-year-old boy presents to the GP with recurrent chest infections and poor growth and weight gain. The patient is referred by the GP to a paediatric clinic, who order further tests including a genetic test for mutations in the CFTR gene to screen for cystic fibrosis. This confirms a single nucleotide mutation in the CFTR gene resulting in a stop codon in place of arginine. What is the name of this type of mutation?
explanation:
Nonsense mutation
Nonsense - a mutation that results in a stop codon. Cystic fibrosis is a genetic condition caused by mutations in the CF transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene, causing chiefly recurrent respiratory infections, pancreatic insufficiency and diabetes. In around 10% of cases it may be caused by a nonsense mutation, whereby a single nucleotide base change means a stop codon is coded in place of an amino acid residue. This can have profound implications on the protein transcription and phenotype of that gene and occurs in approximately 5% of single nucleotide mutations.

Frameshift mutation
A frameshift mutation is an insertion or deletion of a number of nucleotide bases that cause a change in the 3-base reading frame of codons for transcription. For example, if the base C was deleted from the sequence TTCAGAA, the first two codons would change from 'TTC' and 'AGA' to 'TTA' and 'GAA'. This changes the amino acids from phenylalanine and arginine to leucine and glutamic acid. The changes in amino acids transcribed can have very drastic effects on the subsequent proteins and functions thereof. Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an example of a condition that can be caused by this sort of mutation.

Missense mutation
A missense mutation refers to a single base change in a codon that changes the amino acid residue. These occur in 70% of single base mutations. This can have effects on structure and function of the transcribed protein, and cause pathology such as the inactivation of tumour suppressor genes. Conversely, amino acid changes can be neutral and not affect protein function.

Silent mutation
A silent mutation describes a single base mutation where the amino acid does not alter despite the altered codon - for example, both codons UGU and UGC code for cysteine. This property of the genetic code that multiple codons can code for the same amino acid is termed 'degeneracy'. This type of mutation is 'silent' when that the same protein is translated and there is no effect on the downstream processing or phenotype of the gene.

Synonymous mutation
A synonymous mutation is a single base change that does not alter the amino acid (as in silent mutations). However, a synonymous mutation does cause other changes in downstream processing (transcription, splicing, translation) or phenotype of the gene. Phenylketonuria and von Hippel-Lindau disease are examples of conditions that can be caused by this type of mutation.

stem: A study evaluates the long-term survival of patients with early-stage breast cancer treated with either chemotherapy alone or chemotherapy combined with targeted radiotherapy. The primary endpoint was overall mortality. The hazard ratio for mortality in the combined therapy group compared to chemotherapy alone is reported as 0.70 (95% CI: 0.55–0.85). Which conclusion can be drawn from this study?
options: Combined therapy increases mortality by 30% compared to chemotherapy alone
Combined therapy lowers mortality risk by 30% compared to chemotherapy alone
Combined therapy reduces mortality by 70% compared to chemotherapy alone
Combined therapy reduces mortality by 70% in all patients
Mortality risk is the same in both groups
explanation:
Combined therapy lowers mortality risk by 30% compared to chemotherapy alone
The hazard ratio (HR) of 0.70 indicates that patients receiving combined therapy have a 30% lower risk of mortality compared to those on chemotherapy alone. The HR represents the relative risk, meaning the mortality risk in the combined therapy group is 70% of that in the chemotherapy-only group, translating to a 30% reduction in risk (calculated as 1 - 0.70 = 0.30). The 95% confidence interval (CI: 0.55–0.85) does not include 1, confirming statistical significance and ruling out the possibility of no effect. These findings suggest that combined therapy significantly improves survival, which is essential for treatment planning in early-stage breast cancer.

Combined therapy increases mortality by 30% compared to chemotherapy alone
An HR of 0.70 indicates a decrease, not an increase, in mortality risk. A 30% increase in mortality would correspond to an HR greater than 1 (e.g., HR = 1.30). Since the HR is below 1, it signifies a protective effect of combined therapy. If the HR had been above 1, it would indicate a higher mortality risk, which is not the case in this study.

Combined therapy reduces mortality by 70% compared to chemotherapy alone
An HR of 0.70 corresponds to a 30% reduction in mortality risk, not 70%. A 70% reduction would require an HR of 0.30 (since 1 - 0.30 = 0.70). Misinterpreting the HR in this way would overstate the survival benefit of combined therapy. The correct interpretation is that combined therapy lowers mortality risk by 30%, as confirmed by the study data.

Combined therapy reduces mortality by 70% in all patients
The HR of 0.70 reflects a 30% reduction in relative risk, not a 70% reduction in all patients. The HR represents an average effect within the study population, but individual patient responses may vary. Additionally, the confidence interval (0.55–0.85) suggests variability in the actual effect. While combined therapy improves survival, the degree of benefit can differ based on factors such as age, tumour biology, and comorbidities.

Mortality risk is the same in both groups
If mortality risk were the same, the HR would be 1.00, indicating no difference between groups. Since the HR is 0.70, it confirms that combined therapy reduces mortality risk compared to chemotherapy alone. The 95% CI (0.55–0.85) does not include 1, meaning this difference is statistically significant. If the HR had been close to 1 with a wide confidence interval, it might indicate no meaningful difference, but that is not the case here.

stem: Which one of the following statements regarding leptin is incorrect?
options: Is produced mainly by the hypothalamus
Stimulates the release of melanocyte-stimulating hormone
Obese patients have higher leptin levels
Plays a key role in the regulation of body weight
explanation:
Is produced mainly by the hypothalamus
Leptin is secreted by adipose tissue. Is produced mainly by the hypothalamus is the incorrect statement, making it the correct answer to this question. Leptin is not primarily produced by the hypothalamus; it is predominantly secreted by adipocytes (fat cells) in white adipose tissue. The amount of leptin produced is directly proportional to the amount of fat tissue in the body. The hypothalamus is actually a target for leptin action rather than its source.

Stimulates the release of melanocyte-stimulating hormone
Stimulates the release of melanocyte-stimulating hormone is a correct statement. When leptin binds to its receptors in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus, it activates proopiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons. These neurons produce α-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (αMSH), which then acts on melanocortin-4 receptors (MC4R) to decrease appetite and increase energy expenditure. This is one of the key pathways through which leptin exerts its anorexigenic (appetite-suppressing) effects.

Obese patients have higher leptin levels
Obese patients have higher leptin levels is a correct statement. Since leptin is produced by adipose tissue, individuals with more fat mass have higher circulating leptin levels. Paradoxically, despite these elevated leptin levels, obese individuals do not experience the expected decrease in appetite or increase in energy expenditure. This phenomenon is known as leptin resistance, where the brain becomes less responsive to leptin signalling, similar to insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes.

Plays a key role in the regulation of body weight
Plays a key role in the regulation of body weight is a correct statement. Leptin is a crucial hormone in the complex system that regulates energy homeostasis and body weight. It acts as a signal from adipose tissue to the brain about the body's energy stores. When functioning properly, this feedback loop helps maintain stable body weight by adjusting food intake and energy expenditure. Genetic mutations in the leptin gene or leptin receptor gene can lead to severe early-onset obesity, further demonstrating leptin's essential role in weight regulation.

High levels decrease appetite
High levels decrease appetite is a correct statement. Under normal physiological conditions, increased leptin levels signal to the brain that energy stores are sufficient, leading to decreased appetite and increased energy expenditure. This occurs through multiple pathways in the hypothalamus, including the stimulation of anorexigenic POMC neurons and inhibition of orexigenic (appetite-stimulating) neuropeptide Y (NPY) and agouti-related peptide (AgRP) neurons. However, as mentioned earlier, in obesity, this mechanism becomes impaired due to leptin resistance.

stem: A researcher is designing a trial to investigate the use of a novel drug for patients admitted with severe COVID-19. The hypothesis (H1) is that the drug will improve in-hospital mortality in patients admitted with severe COVID-19. The null hypothesis (H0) is that the drug will not improve in-hospital mortality in patients admitted with severe COVID-19. The team want to ensure that the study has sufficient power to answer the clinical research question. A table is constructed to consider the possible outcomes of the study. Study accepts H0 Study rejects H0 Reality H0 Box A Box B Reality H1 Box C Box D Which of the following represents the power of the study?
explanation:
The value of Box D
The power of a study is the probability of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis when it is false. The table below shows the possible outcomes of a study (accepting/rejecting the null hypothesis H0 in relation to reality - whether the H0 is true or not. Study accepts H0 Reality H0 Reality H1 Study rejects H0 Type 1 error (alpha) Type 2 error (beta) Power (1-beta) Alpha (α) and beta (β) are set by the study designers then a calculation of the required study sample size can be done using the difference between groups that the study is trying to detect. The typical level of α is 0.05, which represents a 5% probability of a type 1 error (rejecting the null hypothesis when it is in fact correct). β is the probability of a type II error (accepting the null hypothesis when it is in fact incorrect). β is typically set at 0.8. β and power sum to 1. Therefore power = 1 - β. Power could be described as '1 - the value of Box C', which is the same as saying power = 1 - the probability of a type II error. The statement 'power = 1 + the value of Box D' would be incorrect.

The value of Box A
The value of Box A represents the probability of correctly accepting the null hypothesis when it is true (1 - α). This is not the power of the study.

The value of Box B
The value of Box B represents the probability of a type I error (α), which is the probability of incorrectly rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true. This is not the power of the study.

The value of Box C
The value of Box C represents the probability of a type II error (β), which is the probability of incorrectly accepting the null hypothesis when it is false. Power is 1 - β, not β itself.

1 + the value of Box D
The statement 'power = 1 + the value of Box D' is incorrect. Power is 1 - β, not 1 + β.

stem: Which one of the following foods is the best source of folic acid?
explanation:
Liver
The correct answer is Liver. Liver, particularly beef liver, is one of the richest dietary sources of folic acid. Folic acid, also known as folate or vitamin B9, plays a crucial role in many bodily functions including DNA synthesis and repair, cell division, and growth. It's also essential for the production of red blood cells and preventing anemia.

Cheese
Cheese contains some amount of folic acid but it is not as high as in liver. Cheese is a good source of calcium and protein but it doesn't provide enough folic acid to meet daily requirements.

Red meat
Red meat, while rich in protein and iron, does not contain significant amounts of folic acid. It should be noted that consuming high amounts of red meat has been linked to certain health risks such as heart disease and colon cancer.

Fish
Fish, specifically fatty fish like salmon and mackerel, are excellent sources of omega-3 fatty acids which are beneficial for heart health. However, they do not contain substantial amounts of folic acid.

Milk
Milk is a good source of several nutrients including calcium and vitamin D but it's not a significant source of folic acid. Some types of milk can be fortified with folic acid but it's naturally occurring levels are relatively low.

stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of ischemic heart disease presents to the clinic complaining of frequent episodes of chest discomfort, particularly during physical activity. He describes the discomfort as a tightness in the chest that is relieved by rest. The GP starts an as-required medication to be taken to relieve the chest pain and refers the patient to a rapid-access cardiology clinic. Which of the following best explains the dual action of this as-required medication?
options: Decreases myocardial contractility and decreases heart rate
Decreases systemic vascular resistance and inhibits leukocyte activation
Increases coronary blood flow and stimulates fibrinolysis
Relaxes vascular smooth muscle and inhibits platelet aggregation
Relieves coronary vasospasm and promotes endothelial repair
explanation:
Relaxes vascular smooth muscle and inhibits platelet aggregation
Nitric oxide - vasodilation + inhibits platelet aggregation. Relaxes vascular smooth muscle and inhibits platelet aggregation is correct. The medication described is GTN, a prodrug of nitric oxide (NO), a potent vasodilator and antithrombotic agent. NO activates guanylyl cyclase in vascular smooth muscle cells, increasing cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) levels. This reduces intracellular calcium, leading to the relaxation of vascular smooth muscle and subsequent vasodilation. In addition, NO inhibits platelet activation and aggregation via cGMP-dependent pathways.

Decreases myocardial contractility and decreases heart rate
Decreases myocardial contractility and reduces heart rate is incorrect. NO does not directly affect myocardial contractility or heart rate. These effects are mediated by beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers, not NO. NO primarily acts on vascular smooth muscle and platelets.

Decreases systemic vascular resistance and inhibits leukocyte activation
Decreases systemic vascular resistance and inhibits leukocyte activation is incorrect. While NO reduces systemic vascular resistance through vasodilation, it does not primarily affect leukocyte activation. NO’s anti-inflammatory properties are minor compared to its vasodilatory and antiplatelet effects.

Increases coronary blood flow and stimulates fibrinolysis
Increases coronary blood flow and stimulates fibrinolysis is incorrect. NO increases coronary blood flow via vasodilation, but it does not directly stimulate fibrinolysis. Fibrinolysis involves plasmin activation and fibrin degradation, which are not directly mediated by NO.

Relieves coronary vasospasm and promotes endothelial repair
Relieves coronary vasospasm and promotes endothelial repair is incorrect. While NO helps relieve coronary vasospasm by relaxing smooth muscle, it does not actively promote endothelial repair. Endothelial repair is mediated by growth factors and cellular regeneration, independent of NO.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents with bleeding gums and a rash. On examination, you note a perifollicular petechial rash on his lower extremities. Blood results are as follows: Hb 110 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 282 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 8.2 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) MCV 85 fl (80 - 100) Blood film Occasional hyperchromic spherocytes What is the likely cause?
explanation:
Ascorbic acid deficiency
Bleeding gums and receding, think scurvy. Ascorbic acid deficiency is correct. The clinical features of bleeding gums and a perifollicular petechial rash are classic of scurvy. Mild anaemia can also occur as demonstrated in this case.

Auto immune haemolytic anaemia
Auto immune haemolytic anaemia is incorrect. Although the patient has anaemia, the clinical features are more in keeping with scurvy.

B12 deficiency
B12 deficiency is incorrect. B12 deficiency presents with macrocytosis and in severe cases anaemia, thrombocytopenia and leukopenia. Furthermore, it would not explain the gum bleeding and rash.

Folate deficiency
Folate deficiency is incorrect. Folate deficiency presents with macrocytosis and in severe cases anaemia, thrombocytopenia and leukopenia. Furthermore, it would not explain the gum bleeding and rash.

Hereditary spherocytosis
Hereditary spherocytosis is incorrect. Although the patient has anaemia, the clinical features are more in keeping with scurvy. Although spherocytes are present on the blood film, these can also be seen in scurvy.

stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding X-linked recessive inheritance?
options: A female child of a heterozygous female carrier has a 50% chance of being a carrier
50% of the male offspring of affected males will manifest the disease
An affected child's uncle on the paternal side will also manifest the disease
50% of the female offspring of affected males will be carriers
explanation:
A female child of a heterozygous female carrier has a 50% chance of being a carrier
The correct answer is A female child of a heterozygous female carrier has a 50% chance of being a carrier. This is true because in X-linked recessive inheritance, females have two X chromosomes and thus can be carriers without showing the disease phenotype. If a female is heterozygous for an X-linked recessive trait, she will pass on the affected X chromosome to approximately half of her offspring. Therefore, each female child has a 50% probability of inheriting the affected gene and thus being a carrier.

An example is Friedreich's ataxia
An example is Friedreich's ataxia is incorrect. Friedreich's ataxia is an example of autosomal recessive inheritance, not X-linked recessive inheritance. It means that this disorder affects both sexes equally and requires two copies of the mutated gene, one from each parent, to manifest the disease.

50% of the male offspring of affected males will manifest the disease
50% of the male offspring of affected males will manifest the disease is also incorrect. In fact, none of the male offspring from an affected male will inherit the disease because males pass on their Y chromosome to their sons, not their X chromosome which carries the mutation.

An affected child's uncle on the paternal side will also manifest the disease
The statement An affected child's uncle on the paternal side will also manifest the disease is false as well. In X-linked recessive inheritance diseases, an affected male cannot pass on his condition to his nephews through his brothers since he passes his Y chromosome to his sons who are their fathers.

50% of the female offspring of affected males will be carriers
50% of the female offspring of affected males will be carriers is wrong because all female offspring (100%) from an affected father would be carriers. This occurs because daughters always receive their father's single X chromosome which carries the mutation in case he suffers from an X-linked recessive disorder.

stem: A pharmaceutical company aims to develop a new screening test to establish the risk of pancreatic cancer. They are currently establishing multiple screening test statistics to build up a report for marketing purposes. They are using a sample size of 500 patients of which 100 patients tested negative for pancreatic cancer. Out of these 100 patients, 25 are subsequently diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. Out of the remaining 400 patients who tested positive, 350 patients had the diagnosis. What is the specificity of this screening test?
explanation:
0.60
Specificity = TN / (TN + FP) 0.60 is the correct answer. Specificity is defined as the proportion of patients without the condition that has a negative screening test result. We can establish this by putting the values in a table as seen below. Disease present
disease absent
Tested positive
350
50
Tested negative
25
75
As we already know 100 patients tested negative for the screening test and 25 of these patients had pancreatic cancer, we know that 75 patients tested negative but did not have the diagnosis. Through this, we can calculate that 125 patients did not have the diagnosis and 75 of these patients tested negative as we know that 350 who tested positive had the diagnosis. Specificity is calculated through patients who tested negative over a total number of patients who did not have the diagnosis resulting in the value 75/125 = 0.60.

0.75
0.75 is incorrect. This value is the negative predictive value. This is a relative chance of the patients not having a condition should they test negative. This is calculated through the patients who tested negative and do not have pancreatic cancer over the total number of patients who tested negative. This would be 75/100 = 0.75.

0.88
0.88 is incorrect. This value is a positive predictive value. Similar to above however this is the relative chance of the patient having the condition if they have a positive result. Using the table above this would be the number of patients with a positive result and have pancreatic cancer (350), over the total number of patients who tested positive (400). Therefore this would be 350/400=0.88.

0.93
0.93 is incorrect. This is the sensitivity. This is essentially the opposite of specificity in that it calculated the proportion of patients who have the condition and have a positive test result. This would be 350 patients who have pancreatic cancer and have a positive test, over the total number of patients with pancreatic cancer (375). This would be 350/375=0.95.

2.33
2.33 is incorrect. This is the value for the likelihood ratio for a positive test result. This is calculated through the sensitivity /1- specificity.

stem: A 48-year-old woman is admitted following presentation to the emergency department with a 5 day history of severe vomiting and diarrhoea following a recent trip to Africa. She feels weak and lethargic, and has been struggling to keep down food and drink. On initial assessment, she has dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, cool extremities and a non-visible jugular venous pressure. She is producing dark brown urine and is clinically oliguric over 24 hour measurement. Her initial blood tests reveal: Urea 33 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 320 µmol/L (55 - 120) She is given fluid therapy and antibiotic treatment for her gastroenteritis. Three days later she appears clinically rehydrated, and is apyrexial, but still oliguric, however her blood tests reveal: Urea 39 mmol/L (2.0 - 7.0) Creatinine 510 µmol/L (55 - 120) Urinalysis and microscopy reveals muddy brown granular casts. What is the cause of her deteriorating urea and creatinine?
explanation:
Acute tubular necrosis
Acute tubular necrosis is associated with granular, muddy-brown urinary casts. This patient has experienced a prolonged period of dehydration and prerenal acute kidney injury (AKI) secondary to bacterial gastroenteritis. Hypovolaemia reduces glomerular perfusion and filtration rates, which over time causes renal cell hypoxia and necrosis of the renal tubular epithelium. This is the mechanism of renal injury in this case, but acute tubular necrosis (ATN) can arise from other means e.g. sepsis or nephrotoxic agents. This patient has signs that suggest ATN as the aetiology of unresolving renal dysfunction despite fluid therapy. These include: granular renal cell casts, which are collections of dead renal tubular cells sloughing in the tubular lumen, and a normal urea:creatinine ratio with both raised above baseline. This would not be seen in pre-renal AKI, which features a raised urea:creatinine ratio due to enhanced passive proximal reabsorption of urea that accompanies sodium in a hypovolaemic state.

Obstructive uropathy
Given that this patient is still passing urine, but is only oliguric, suggests it is unlikely to be a bilateral obstruction. While it is possible that there is a unilateral obstruction, the history points more towards acute tubular necrosis as the predominant cause of renal injury.

Ongoing pre-renal AKI
This patient has definitely had a pre-renal AKI contributing to deranged initial renal function results. However, the failure to respond to fluids is a hallmark that hypovolaemia is no longer the direct cause of renal injury, and that the dysfunction is now intrinsic to the renal parenchyma itself.

Glomerulonephritis
While glomerulonephritis is a cause of intrinsic renal dysfunction, it is typically slower in onset and does not usually occur on the background of ongoing pre-renal AKI, rather on the background of secondary disease or in the presence of toxic drugs. While the syndrome is indeed vast, it is typically associated with proteinuria, haematuria or both, neither of which are displayed here.

Acute interstitial nephritis
While it is an excellent thought that both the gastrointestinal bacterial infection as well as the antibiotic therapy could cause acute interstitial nephritis, the classic triad of rash, fever and eosinophilia are all not present. Moreover, the urine sediment, if present, is more likely to be white cell (and/or red cell) casts/pyuria.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with pleuritic chest pain. Her Wells' score for pulmonary embolism (PE) is 1, indicating a low pre-test probability. A D-dimer test is performed. D-dimer 210 ng/mL FEU (< 500) The result is negative and PE is considered to be excluded. What is meant by the negative predictive value of this test?
options: The proportion of patients with the condition who test positive
The proportion of patients without the condition who test negative
The probability that the patient has the condition given a positive test
The probability that the patient does not have the condition given a negative test
The probability that a test result is the same upon re-testing
explanation:
The probability that the patient does not have the condition given a negative test
Negative predictive value - the chance that the patient does not have the condition if the diagnostic test is negative. The probability that the patient does not have the condition given a negative test. This is the correct definition of Negative Predictive Value (NPV). In this clinical scenario, the patient has a low pre-test probability of pulmonary embolism (PE), and the D-dimer test is negative. The D-dimer test is highly sensitive for PE, meaning it is very good at detecting the disease when it is present. Consequently, a negative result in a low-risk patient has a very high NPV (typically >99%). This means there is a very high probability that this patient does not have a PE, given her negative test result. This high NPV is the statistical basis for using the D-dimer test to rule out PE in low-risk populations, as recommended by NICE guidelines, thereby avoiding further imaging like a CTPA and its associated radiation exposure.

The proportion of patients with the condition who test positive
The proportion of patients with the condition who test positive. This is the definition of sensitivity. Sensitivity measures a test's ability to correctly identify patients who have the disease. It is calculated as True Positives / (True Positives + False Negatives). The D-dimer test has high sensitivity for PE, meaning that if a patient truly has a PE, the D-dimer is very likely to be positive. However, this option defines sensitivity, not the negative predictive value, which is what the question asks for.

The proportion of patients without the condition who test negative
The proportion of patients without the condition who test negative. This is the definition of specificity. Specificity measures a test's ability to correctly identify patients who do not have the disease. It is calculated as True Negatives / (True Negatives + False Positives). The D-dimer test has low specificity, as many conditions other than PE (e.g., infection, inflammation, malignancy, recent surgery, pregnancy) can cause a raised D-dimer. This means a positive result does not specifically indicate PE. This option defines specificity, not negative predictive value.

The probability that the patient has the condition given a positive test
The probability that the patient has the condition given a positive test. This is the definition of Positive Predictive Value (PPV). PPV tells you the likelihood that a patient with a positive test result actually has the disease. Due to the low specificity of the D-dimer, its PPV for PE is low, especially in low-prevalence populations. A positive D-dimer requires further investigation (e.g., CTPA) to confirm the diagnosis. This is the counterpart to NPV and is not the correct answer.

The probability that a test result is the same upon re-testing
The probability that a test result is the same upon re-testing. This describes the concept of precision or reliability. Precision refers to the consistency and reproducibility of a test. A precise test will yield similar results when performed multiple times on the same sample under the same conditions. While precision is a desirable characteristic of any diagnostic test, it is a measure of the test's performance consistency, not its ability to correctly classify patients based on their disease status. It is therefore distinct from negative predictive value.

stem: A 70-year-old woman has a wide local excision for ductal carcinoma. She attends the oncology clinic and is considered for treatment based on the genetic profile of the tumour - detection of a mutated oncogene is needed. Which technique will most likely be used for this purpose?
explanation:
Polymerase chain reaction
Polymerase chain reactions are used to detect mutated oncogenes. The answer is polymerase chain reaction (PCR) which is used to selectively amplify and detect short genomic sequences. This technique is the most cost effective when considering other possible answers given.

Fluorescence in situ hybridisation
Fluorescence in situ hybridisation uses a labelled probe to detect a genomic sequence on a chromosome and is less sensitive than PCR, and not the choice of test here.

Western blot
Western blot is used to detect a specific protein whereas the question asks about detecting the mutated oncogene.

Enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)
An Enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) is used to measure proteins. It has no role here.

High performance liquid chromatography
High performance liquid chromatography is used to detect molecules like toxin and drugs. Most assays use ELISA rather this technology now.

stem: You are caring for a local cardiology consultant's father who has been admitted following a myocardial infarction. He bleeps you from the switchboard and asks how his father is doing. You recognise his voice on the phone. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Decline to give any details over the phone but offer to meet the consultant face-to-face for a chat
As a matter of professional courtesy ask for his advice on postmyocardial infarction care
Ask permission from his father then give relevant details
Give full details, include the troponin I value and offer to fax the ECG
explanation:
Ask permission from his father then give relevant details
The main nub of this question relates to confidentiality. You cannot give details over the phone to anyone, even his son, without the patient's express permission. Whilst it may be presumed that this is what the patient would want it is impossible to be sure of the family dynamics. If the patient has given permission and you are sure you are speaking to the son then giving relevant details is the best option.

Decline to give any details over the phone but offer to meet the consultant face-to-face for a chat
Asking the consultant to come in as an option but may not be necessary if the previous conditions are met.

As a matter of professional courtesy ask for his advice on postmyocardial infarction care
Involving a relative in the management of a patient is inappropriate and the worst option.

Give full details, include the troponin I value and offer to fax the ECG
Giving details without first getting permission from the patient is breaking confidentiality, however well intentioned.

Say he is 'doing fine'
Saying he is 'doing fine' is unlikely to satisfy a consultant cardiologist.

stem: A 25-year-old man attends with a 3-month history of numbness in his right hand. On examination, you note the loss of sensation to the palmar and dorsal aspect of the 5th digit. Sensation of the forearm is preserved. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cubital tunnel syndrome
Cubital tunnel syndrome is correct. This is a classical description of ulnar nerve neuropathy. The ulnar nerve supplies sensory innervation to the palmar and dorsal aspects of 1.5 fingers medially. It has a motor component which can result in wasting and paralysis of intrinsic hand muscles (except lateral two lumbricals) and the hypothenar muscles. Froment's test can be used to test the function of the adductor pollicis muscle which is often weak in ulnar neuropathy.

Axillary nerve neuropathy
Axillary nerve neuropathy is incorrect. The axillary nerve has both a motor and a sensory distribution of innervation. It has motor fibres that innervate the deltoid muscle, acting as an abductor, flexor and extensor at the shoulder joint, as well as the teres minor muscle, allowing lateral rotation of the glenohumeral joint. Its sensory function is from the superior lateral cutaneous nerve of arm, which sweeps around the posterior border of the deltoid and supplies the skin over the lower two-thirds of the posterior part of this muscle, as well as that covering the long head of the triceps brachii.

C8/T1 radiculopathy
C8/T1 radiculopathy is incorrect. C8/T1 radiculopathy can mimic ulnar nerve neuropathy. In this case, the preserved sensation of the forearm favours a diagnosis of cubital tunnel syndrome. The ulnar nerve does not provide sensation to the medial forearm, which is innervated by the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve (C8 and T1).

Carpal tunnel syndrome
Carpal tunnel syndrome is incorrect. Median nerve dysfunction results in carpal tunnel syndrome characterised by sensory loss over the lateral 3.5 digits, and loss of motor function to the flexor muscles of the forearm and hand as well as those muscles responsible for flexion, abduction, opposition, and extension of the thumb.

Radial nerve neuropathy
Radial nerve neuropathy is incorrect. The radial nerve innervates the muscles located in the posterior arm and posterior forearm. Dysfunction, therefore, results in loss of elbow and wrist extension. It also supplies sensation to the postero-lateral aspect of the hand.

stem: Which one of the following immunological changes is seen in progressive HIV infection?
options: A rise in the CD4/CD8 ratio
explanation:
Increase in B2-microglobulin levels
The correct answer is an increase in B2-microglobulin levels. Beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) is a component of the MHC class I molecules, which are present on all nucleated cells. In HIV infection, there is a high rate of cellular turnover and immune activation, leading to increased shedding of B2M into the bloodstream. Therefore, serum B2M levels are elevated and correlate with disease progression.

Increase in IL-2 production
An increase in IL-2 production is not typically seen in progressive HIV infection. Interleukin 2 (IL-2) is a cytokine that stimulates the growth and differentiation of T cells. In HIV infection, IL-2 production may initially increase as part of the immune response; however, as the disease progresses and CD4+ T cells are depleted, IL-2 production decreases.

Increased type IV hypersensitivity responses
Increased type IV hypersensitivity responses are also not characteristic of progressive HIV infection. Type IV hypersensitivity reactions involve T cell-mediated immune responses. While these may be heightened early in HIV infection as the immune system attempts to combat the virus, over time and with progressive immunosuppression, these responses become blunted.

Increased natural killer (NK) cell function
Increased natural killer (NK) cell function is not typically seen during progressive HIV infection. NK cells are part of the innate immune response and can kill virus-infected cells without prior sensitisation. However, their function may be impaired in advanced stages of HIV due to generalised immunosuppression.

A rise in the CD4/CD8 ratio
A rise in the CD4/CD8 ratio does not occur in progressive HIV infection; rather the opposite is true. The CD4/CD8 ratio usually falls below 1 as CD4+ T cell counts decrease more rapidly than CD8+ T cell counts due to direct targeting by HIV.

stem: In the UK, we have numerous screening programmes for important health issues such as breast cancer. A new screening test for breast cancer is being evaluated compared to the conventional use of mammography. There are concerns this test appears to lengthen survival as the breast cancer is picked up at an earlier stage but the overall outcome remains unchanged. What type of bias is this?
explanation:
Lead time bias
Lead-time bias - occurs when two tests for a disease are compared, the new test diagnoses the disease earlier, but there is no effect on the outcome of the disease

Length time bias
Length time bias occurs where a disease may progress at different rates therefore slower growing or less aggressive disease has more opportunity to be picked up via screening than aggressive/fast-developing disease.

Self selection bias
Self-selection or volunteer bias is due to the fact that people who tend to engage in screening programmes are not representative of the population (if they take part in screening, they will usually be of a higher socio-economic stance and practice other lifestyle choices that will improve their health as well as screening).

Procedure Bias
Procedure bias is usually related to comparative studies. It is where patients are treated differently depending on their group allocation.

Recall Bias
Recall bias is where the accuracy of data is affected by the retrospective collection. For example, if you were looking at past asbestos exposure, a patient may not be able to recall the exact years they may have been exposed.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with epigastric pain. The pre-test probability of acute pancreatitis is estimated to be 20%. A new rapid test is performed which is negative. This test has a sensitivity of 80% and a specificity of 90% for acute pancreatitis. What are the approximate post-test odds of him having acute pancreatitis?
explanation:
1:18
1:18 is the correct answer. This question requires a three-step calculation to determine how a negative test result modifies the likelihood of a disease. First, the pre-test probability must be converted to pre-test odds. The formula for this is Odds = Probability / (1 - Probability). With a pre-test probability of 20% (or 0.2), the pre-test odds are 0.2 / (1 - 0.2) = 0.2 / 0.8 = 0.25, which can be expressed as a ratio of 1:4. Second, the likelihood ratio for a negative test result (LR-) must be calculated. The LR- indicates how much the odds of the disease decrease when a test is negative. The formula is LR- = (1 - sensitivity) / specificity. Using the values given, LR- = (1 - 0.80) / 0.90 = 0.2 / 0.9 ≈ 0.222. Finally, the posttest odds are calculated by multiplying the pre-test odds by the likelihood ratio: Post-test odds = Pre-test odds × LR- = 0.25 × 0.222 ≈ 0.0555. To express this as a ratio, we can take its reciprocal (1 / 0.0555 ≈ 18), giving post-test odds of approximately 1:18. This demonstrates that the negative test result has significantly reduced the odds of the patient having acute pancreatitis from 1 in 4 to approximately 1 in 18.

2:1
2:1 is incorrect. This value is derived from incorrectly using the likelihood ratio for a positive test (LR+) instead of a negative one. The LR+ is calculated as sensitivity / (1 - specificity), which in this case would be 0.80 / (1 - 0.90) = 0.8 / 0.1 = 8. Multiplying the pre-test odds (0.25) by this LR+ gives post-test odds of 2 (or 2:1). This would be the correct calculation if the patient's test result had been positive. However, the scenario explicitly states the test was negative, so the odds of disease should decrease, not increase.

1:4
1:4 is incorrect. This represents the pre-test odds of the patient having acute pancreatitis before the diagnostic test was performed. A pre-test probability of 20% is equivalent to odds of 1:4. Selecting this option implies that the negative test result had no impact on the likelihood of the disease. Any diagnostic test with a sensitivity and specificity that are not random will alter the pre-test probability. The purpose of performing the test is to refine this initial estimate, so the post-test odds must be different from the pre-test odds.

1:9
1:9 is incorrect. This result likely arises from a miscalculation of the likelihood ratio. One common error is to invert the terms for the LR-, for example by calculating it as (1 - specificity) / (1 - sensitivity). This would yield 0.1 / 0.2 = 0.5. Multiplying the pre-test odds of 0.25 by this incorrect LR of 0.5 gives post-test odds of 0.125, which is a ratio of 1:8. This is very close to 1:9 and represents a plausible but incorrect calculation. It is crucial to use the correct formula for the likelihood ratio to ensure an accurate assessment of post-test probability.

1:22
1:22 is incorrect. While this is numerically close to the correct answer, it likely stems from a rounding error or a slight miscalculation during the process. For example, if the LR- of 0.222 was incorrectly rounded down to 0.2, the post-test odds would be 0.25 x 0.2 = 0.05, which corresponds to 1:20. Alternatively, if the pre-test probability was misremembered as slightly lower, it could also lead to this result. In statistical questions, precision is important, and 1:18 is the most accurate answer derived from the provided figures.

stem: A 34-year-old man is referred to ophthalmology following a deterioration in his vision. He is noted to be tall with thin, long fingers and a degree of learning disabilities. Following review he is suspected as having a displacement of his lens on the right side. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Homocystinuria
Tall, long fingered, downward lens dislocation, learning difficulties, DVT - homocystinuria The presence of learning difficulties points to a diagnosis of homocystinuria rather than Marfan's syndrome.

Marfan's syndrome
The presence of learning difficulties points to a diagnosis of homocystinuria rather than Marfan's syndrome.

stem: What is the most common cardiac defect seen in patients with Down's syndrome?
explanation:
Endocardial cushion defect
Atrioventricular septal defects are the most common congenital cardiac abnormality in Down's syndrome. The correct answer is Endocardial cushion defect, also known as atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD) or atrioventricular canal defect. This occurs in approximately 40-50% of patients with Down's syndrome who have congenital heart disease. The defect results from incomplete fusion of the endocardial cushions during cardiac development, leading to abnormalities of the atrioventricular septum and valves. This creates both atrial and ventricular communication and often involves abnormalities of the mitral and tricuspid valves.

Ventricular septal defect
Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is indeed common in Down's syndrome, occurring in about 35% of cases with cardiac defects, but it is not the most frequent. VSDs occur due to incomplete closure of the interventricular septum during cardiac development, resulting in left-to-right shunting of blood.

Secundum atrial septal defect
Secundum atrial septal defect occurs in approximately 8% of Down's syndrome patients with cardiac defects. This defect involves a hole in the septum secundum portion of the interatrial septum, allowing communication between the right and left atria.

Tetralogy of Fallot
Tetralogy of Fallot is seen in only about 4% of Down's syndrome patients with cardiac defects. This complex condition comprises four abnormalities: pulmonary stenosis, VSD, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy.

Patent ductus arteriosus
Patent ductus arteriosus occurs in approximately 7% of Down's syndrome patients with cardiac defects. This represents persistence of the foetal connection between the pulmonary artery and aorta, which normally closes shortly after birth. While significant in Down's syndrome, it is not the most common cardiac defect in this population.

stem: A new test for lung cancer has a specificity of 95% and a sensitivity of 98%. A thousand people without lung cancer undergo the new test. Which of the following is the number of people who will test negative?
explanation:
950
Specificity is the proportion of patients without the condition who have a negative test result. The test has a specificity of 95%, which means that 95% of the nondiseased people who take the test will correctly have a negative test result. If 1000 people without lung cancer take the test, then 95% of these would test negative (true-negative). 95% of 1000 = (95/100)*1000 = 950.

50
Fifty people without lung cancer will test positive despite not having the disease (false-positive).

stem: A research group evaluating the effectiveness of the pneumococcal vaccine in reducing the rates of pneumococcal pneumonia. A group of 100 volunteers was recruited. Half of the volunteers were given a course of the pneumococcal vaccination. The other half of the volunteers were given placebos. The group was followed-up over the next 12 months following vaccination. Sputum samples were collected if a volunteer developed pneumonia to determine if Streptococcus pneumonia was the cause of pneumonia. Results were divided into 3 categories: volunteers who did not develop pneumonia, volunteers who developed pneumococcal pneumonia and volunteers who developed non-pneumococcal pneumonia. At the end of the year, the results obtained were as follows: Outcome Vaccinated volunteers Unvaccinated volunteers Pneumococcal pneumonia 10 20 Non-pneumococcal pneumonia 6 10 No pneumonia 34 20 The researchers are unsure of the significance of the results obtained. Which of the following statistical tests would be most appropriate?
explanation:
Pearson's chi-square test
Chi-squared test - used to compare proportions or percentages e.g. compares the percentage of patients who improved following two different interventions. This study is looking to assess the efficacy of the new vaccine by comparing the rates of pneumonia between 2 independent groups (vaccinated vs unvaccinated group). The outcome of the study could be described as categorical nominal data as the results can be divided into 3 separate categories. The chi-square test is the most appropriate in this case because the tested groups are independent of each other and the results obtained are nominal.

Independent t-test
Independent t-test should not be used in this case as this requires the resultant data to be continuous and normally distributed in nature (for example blood pressure and heart rate).

McNemar's test
Paired t-test, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and McNemar's test are useful in the comparison of results within paired samples. For example, the paired t-test can be used in comparing blood pressure before and after an antihypertensive medication was taken for the same patient. As this study is comparing 2 independent groups, none of these tests can be applied.

Paired t-test
Paired t-test, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and McNemar's test are useful in the comparison of results within paired samples. For example, the paired t-test can be used in comparing blood pressure before and after an antihypertensive medication was taken for the same patient. As this study is comparing 2 independent groups, none of these tests can be applied.

Wilcoxon signed-rank test
Paired t-test, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and McNemar's test are useful in the comparison of results within paired samples. For example, the paired t-test can be used in comparing blood pressure before and after an antihypertensive medication was taken for the same patient. As this study is comparing 2 independent groups, none of these tests can be applied.

stem: A 30-year-old male attends the neurology outpatient clinic for the first time after moving to live with his new wife. The referral letter from his previous neurologist details that he presented in adolescence with a myoclonic seizure with associated muscle weakness. His mother had similar issues as a teenager and his father has no medical issues. He is an only child. He was diagnosed with myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibres (MERRF) after a confirmatory muscle biopsy and is on treatment for this. He tells you he now wishes to have children. His wife has no current medical issues. What is the likelihood of his children inheriting his disease?
options: All of his children would be affected
His children would be carriers of the disease, but be asymptomatic
His daughter would inherit the disease
His son would inherit the disease
None of his children will inherit the disease
explanation:
None of his children will inherit the disease
For a man with mitochondrial disease, none of his children will inherit the condition. This is a case of patterns of inheritance of mitochondrial diseases. Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibres (MERRF syndrome) is a mitochondrial disease which predominantly affects the nervous system and muscles. The predominant phenotypic features include myopathy and seizures (mainly generalised myoclonic seizures, but case reports have described many types of both focal and generalised seizures). As detailed below, mitochondrial diseases are inherited from maternal mitochondrial DNA. This means that all children of an affected mother will inherit the disease. Given mitochondrial diseases can't be passed on via paternal sperm, Martin will not pass this onto his children and this should be the advice given.

All of his children would be affected
All his children being affected - this would be applicable if a female with a mitochondrial disease were to have children. All of the mitochondrial DNA would then come from the mother.

His children would be carriers of the disease, but be asymptomatic
His children would be carriers of the disease, but be asymptomatic - this scenario can occur in autosomal recessive conditions.

His daughter would inherit the disease
His daughter would inherit the disease - this could occur in several scenarios. Further reading on autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive inheritance would help further knowledge on this topic. Father to daughter inheritance would not fit the MERRF diagnosis.

His son would inherit the disease
His son would inherit the disease - in cases of males inheriting a disorder from their mother, one could think of X-linked inheritance. Usually, only males are affected and, although affected males may occur in consecutive generations, transmission is always through females. Females, on the other hand, would tend to be asymptomatic carriers as they have a second X chromosome which will often compensate for the problem in the other X chromosome.

stem: What is the main constituent of pulmonary surfactant?
explanation:
Dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine
The correct answer is Dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine (DPPC), which comprises approximately 40-50% of pulmonary surfactant by weight. DPPC is a phospholipid that forms a surface-active monolayer at the air-liquid interface of the alveoli, reducing surface tension and preventing alveolar collapse during expiration. Its unique molecular structure, with two saturated palmitic acid chains, allows for optimal surface tension-lowering properties at body temperature.

Apolipoprotein SP-B
Apolipoprotein SP-B is incorrect. While SP-B is an essential surfactant protein that facilitates the spreading and stability of the surfactant film, it only comprises about 2% of surfactant by weight. SP-B is crucial for surfactant function, but it is not the main constituent.

Phosphatidylglycerol
Phosphatidylglycerol is incorrect. Although phosphatidylglycerol is an important phospholipid component of pulmonary surfactant, it only makes up approximately 7-10% of surfactant by weight. It plays a role in surfactant spreading and interaction with surfactant proteins.

Pulmonary elastase
Pulmonary elastase is incorrect. This is an enzyme produced by neutrophils and is not a component of pulmonary surfactant at all. Instead, it is involved in the breakdown of elastin and can contribute to emphysema when present in excess.

Apolipoprotein SP-A
Apolipoprotein SP-A is incorrect. While SP-A is the most abundant surfactant protein and has important functions in host defence and surfactant homeostasis, it only comprises about 5-6% of surfactant by weight. It is not the main constituent of pulmonary surfactant.

stem: A 27-year-old man presents with a rash that has developed across the body. It is intensely itchy. He has a background of asthma and coeliac disease. On examination, the rash is symmetrical and distributed across the scalp, shoulders, elbows and buttocks. It consists of papules and vesicles on an erythematous base, in clusters. They appear somewhat excoriated. Blood tests demonstrate iron-deficiency anaemia. What is most associated with the rash?
explanation:
HLA-DR3
Dermatitis herpetiformis is associated with HLA-DR3. The rash described here is likely dermatitis herpetiformis, given its appearance and association with coeliac disease. It is more common in men than in women. Of the known HLA antigens (encoded on chromosome 6), dermatitis herpetiformis is most commonly associated with HLA-DR3.

HLA-A3
HLA-A3 is incorrect. This is associated with haemochromatosis, not dermatitis herpetiformis.

HLA-B27
HLA-B27 is typically associated with ankylosing spondylitis and reactive arthritis, not dermatitis herpetiformis.

HLA-B51
HLA-B51 is associated with Bechet's disease. It is not typically linked to dermatitis herpetiformis.

HLA-DR4
HLA-DR4 is associated with type 1 diabetes mellitus. It is also linked to rheumatoid arthritis - specifically, the DRB1 gene.

stem: A new drug is being developed for use in heart conduction disorders. As part of the experimental research, a laboratory scientist records the conduction velocities in different parts of a bovine heart using two electrodes. Following a series of velocity measurements, the scientist marks the part of the heart with two red hat pins where he has measured the highest velocity in the heart at around 4 m/s. What is the most likely location of the red hat pins?
explanation:
Purkinje fibres
The fastest conduction velocities in the heart are in the Purkinje fibres. Purkinje fibres are of large diameter and achieve velocities of 2-4 m/s, the fastest conduction in the heart. This rapid conduction allows coordinated ventricular contraction.

AV node
AV node has the slowest conduction velocity in the heart (0.05 m/s). This conduction delay between the atria and the ventricles facilitates the completion of the ventricular filling from the atrial kick before the ventricular contraction begins.

Bachmann's bundle
Bachmann's bundle is a branch of the anterior inter-nodal tract that conducts electrical impulses from the SA node to the left atrium and thus facilitates coordinated atrial contraction.

Bundle of His
Bundle of His is a group of fast-conducting muscle fibres that serves to transmit electrical impulses from the AV node to the Purkinje fibres at velocities up to 2 m/s. The right and left bundle branches conduct the impulses to the right and left ventricles, respectively.

Myocardium
Myocardium conducts electrical impulses at a slower velocity (0.5 m/s). Premature ventricular complexes originating in the myocardium have widened QRS duration owing to the slow conduction of action potentials from myocyte to myocyte.

stem: A 42-year-old man's prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level is 7.8 ng/mL. He asks you what the chances are that he really has prostate cancer. Which of the following statistical parameters would you need to calculate to answer his question?
explanation:
Positive predictive value
Positive predictive value - the chance that the patient has the condition if the diagnostic test is positive. The chance that a patient with a raised PSA level has prostate cancer is the positive predictive value (PPV) of this test. PPV is the probability that subjects with a positive screening test have the disease.

Positive predictive value = true positives/(true positives+false positives)

Negative predictive value
Negative predictive value (NPV) is the probability that subjects with a negative screening test don't have the disease. NPV is the likelihood that the patient does not have prostate cancer if his PSA levels are low.

Likelihood ratio
The likelihood ratio assesses the value of performing a diagnostic test. It shows how much more likely the person is to get a positive test if he/she has the disease when compared with a person without the disease. If the patient was already diagnosed with prostate cancer, a positive likelihood ratio would have suggested that the probability of the PSA levels being high is higher in patients with prostate cancer than those without prostate cancer.

Sensitivity
Sensitivity is the proportion of patients with the condition who have a positive test result.

Specificity
Specificity is the proportion of patients without the condition who have a negative test result.

stem: What level of evidence does a randomised control trial offer?
explanation:
Ib
The correct answer is Ib. A randomised control trial (RCT) provides level Ib evidence according to the Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine. This level of evidence involves individual randomised trials, which are considered high-quality because they minimise bias through random allocation of interventions.

Ia
Ia is incorrect as it refers to systematic reviews of RCTs. Systematic reviews combine results from multiple studies, increasing the overall sample size and enhancing the statistical power. They provide a more comprehensive analysis than individual RCTs and therefore offer a higher level of evidence.

IIa
IIa is also incorrect as it pertains to systematic reviews of cohort studies. Cohort studies are observational by nature and thus have more potential for bias compared to RCTs. Therefore, although they can provide valuable insights into associations between variables, they do not offer as high a level of evidence as RCTs.

IIb
IIb is incorrect as it represents individual cohort studies or low-quality randomized controlled trials (e.g., < 80% follow-up). These types of studies lack the rigorous design characteristic of higher-quality RCTs and thus provide lower levels of evidence.

IV
IV is incorrect because this level corresponds to case series and poor-quality cohort or case-control studies. These types of studies are even less rigorous in their design and execution than those represented by IIa or IIb, providing even lower levels of evidence than an RCT.

stem: A 24-year-old man presents with a 1-week history of haemoptysis, shortness of breath, and fatigue. Over the same period he has noticed that his urine has become “tea-coloured”. On examination, his oxygen saturation is 93% on air, respiratory rate is 22/min, and blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg. Urinalysis reveals haematuria and proteinuria. A chest X-ray demonstrates bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. Which autoantibody is most likely responsible for this condition?
explanation:
Anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM)
Goodpasture's syndrome is caused by autoantibodies against collagen type IV. Anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) is correct, as this patient’s haemoptysis, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, haematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, and acute onset strongly suggest Goodpasture’s syndrome. The anti-GBM antibodies attack type IV collagen in the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, leading to the simultaneous lung and kidney damage. The young male demographic (24 years old) and acute onset of pulmonary haemorrhage (bilateral infiltrates on chest X-ray) and glomerulonephritis (haematuria, proteinuria, elevated creatinine) strongly fits the picture of Goodpasture's syndrome.

Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP)
Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) is incorrect, as while antiCCP is specific for rheumatoid arthritis, this patient lacks joint pain, synovitis, or erosive arthritis. Rheumatoid arthritis does not cause pulmonary-renal syndrome.

Anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA)
Anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) is incorrect, as anti-dsDNA is characteristic of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), which can cause pulmonary haemorrhage, though rarely. However, SLE typically presents with additional features such as malar rash, joint pain, or cytopenias, absent in this patient.

Anti-myeloperoxidase p-ANCA (anti-MPO)
Anti-myeloperoxidase p-ANCA (anti-MPO) is incorrect, as p-ANCA is most commonly associated with microscopic polyangiitis, which can also cause a pulmonary–renal syndrome. However, microscopic polyangiitis usually evolves over several weeks, with constitutional upset, arthralgia or a small-vessel vasculitic rash; none of these features is evident here. In contrast, anti-GBM disease presents far more abruptly and tends to be more severe in young men.

Cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (c-ANCA)
Cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (c-ANCA) is incorrect, as c-ANCA is associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), another cause of pulmonary-renal syndrome. Although GPA typically involves upper respiratory tract symptoms (sinusitis, nasal involvement) and granulomatous inflammation, these features may occasionally be absent. However, given the clinical scenario, age, and acute presentation without other GPA-related features, anti-GBM remains the more likely diagnosis.

stem: Which one of the following karyotypes is associated with short stature?
explanation:
45,XO
45,XO is the correct karyotype associated with short stature as this represents Turner syndrome. Turner syndrome is characterised by the presence of only one X chromosome (monosomy X) and is associated with several clinical features including short stature, primary amenorrhoea, webbed neck, and coarctation of the aorta. Growth failure is a cardinal feature, with untreated patients typically reaching an adult height of 143-145 cm.

46,YO
46,YO is not a viable karyotype as at least one X chromosome is required for survival. The X chromosome contains essential genes that cannot be compensated for by the Y chromosome.

46,XO
46,XO is an incorrect notation for Turner syndrome. The correct notation is 45,XO, representing the total number of chromosomes (45) followed by the sex chromosome composition.

47,XYY
47,XYY syndrome (Jacob's syndrome) is actually associated with tall stature. Males with this karyotype are typically taller than average and may have learning difficulties, but physical features are usually subtle.

47,XXY
47,XXY (Klinefelter syndrome) is also associated with tall stature rather than short stature. These individuals typically have long legs, gynaecomastia, and small testes with azoospermia. They are often taller than their genetic potential would predict.

stem: A 68-year-old man who lives alone is reviewed on the ward. He reports a diet consisting mainly of bread and tinned soup. Examination reveals swollen, bleeding gums, perifollicular petechiae on his legs, and poor healing of a recent skin tear. His blood tests are as follows: Platelets 250 x 109/L (150 - 400) Prothrombin time 13 seconds (11 - 14) APTT 30 seconds (25 - 35) What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Scurvy
Scurvy is the correct diagnosis. This patient presents with a classic triad of symptoms for vitamin C deficiency: gingival disease (swollen, bleeding gums), skin manifestations (perifollicular petechiae), and impaired wound healing. The social history of living alone combined with a very restricted diet lacking fresh fruit and vegetables provides a strong risk factor. Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is an essential cofactor for the enzymes prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, which are critical for the post-translational modification of collagen. Defective collagen synthesis leads to fragile blood vessels, causing the characteristic bleeding manifestations, and compromises the integrity of connective tissue, resulting in poor wound healing. The normal platelet count and coagulation screen are crucial negative findings that help exclude haematological and other coagulation disorders, pointing towards a nutritional or vessel wall defect.

Acute myeloid leukaemia
Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is an important differential for bleeding and bruising. In AML, bone marrow infiltration by leukaemic blasts leads to bone marrow failure, resulting in pancytopenia. Patients often present with symptoms of anaemia (fatigue), neutropenia (infections), and thrombocytopenia (bruising, petechiae, gingival bleeding). However, this patient has a normal platelet count, which makes a diagnosis of AML highly unlikely. A full blood count would be essential and would be expected to show other abnormalities such as anaemia and a high or low white cell count with circulating blasts.

Disseminated intravascular coagulation
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is a consumptive coagulopathy characterised by widespread activation of the clotting cascade. This leads to the formation of microthrombi and consumption of clotting factors and platelets, resulting in simultaneous thrombosis and bleeding. DIC is typically an acute process triggered by a significant underlying condition such as sepsis, major trauma, or malignancy. The clinical picture would be of a critically unwell patient, and laboratory tests would show thrombocytopenia, prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), and low fibrinogen levels. This patient's subacute presentation and entirely normal coagulation screen rule out DIC.

Periodontitis
Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease of the gums and supporting structures of the teeth. Severe periodontitis can certainly cause swollen, bleeding, and receding gums. However, it is a localised oral condition and would not account for the systemic features seen in this patient, specifically the perifollicular petechiae on his legs and the impaired wound healing of the skin tear on his shin. While he may have co-existing periodontitis, it does not explain the entire clinical picture, which points towards a systemic pathology.

Vitamin K deficiency
Vitamin K deficiency impairs the synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X). This leads to a bleeding diathesis, typically manifesting as easy bruising, melaena, or haematuria. The key laboratory finding is a prolonged prothrombin time (PT), as Factor VII has the shortest half-life and is most sensitive to vitamin K levels. In this patient, the PT is normal, effectively excluding clinically significant vitamin K deficiency as the cause of his symptoms. Furthermore, the specific signs of hypertrophic gingivitis and perifollicular haemorrhage are not typical features of vitamin K deficiency.

stem: Two siblings, a 12-year-old girl and a 15-year-old boy, present with clinical features of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). The girl has multiple café-au-lait spots and two cutaneous neurofibromas but is otherwise healthy with no significant functional impairments. The boy, however, has a more severe presentation, including numerous large neurofibromas, axillary freckling, optic glioma, and scoliosis requiring bracing. Both siblings have been confirmed to carry the same pathogenic mutation in the NF1 gene. What accounts for the varying severities of the condition between the two siblings?
explanation:
Expressivity
In genetics, expressivity describes the extent to which a genotype shows its phenotypic expression in an individual. Expressivity is the correct answer because it explains the varying severity of clinical features observed in the two siblings, despite both carrying the same pathogenic mutation in the NF1 gene. Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is a condition where expressivity is a well-documented phenomenon, with family members often exhibiting a wide range of severity despite sharing the same genetic mutation. In this case, the 12-year-old girl has mild manifestations such as café-au-lait spots and a few cutaneous neurofibromas, whereas her 15-year-old brother has a more severe phenotype, including multiple large neurofibromas, optic glioma, and scoliosis. This variation illustrates the concept of expressivity, which refers to the degree or extent to which a genotype is phenotypically expressed. Factors such as modifier genes, environmental influences, or allelic variation contribute to this variability, resulting in the spectrum of clinical features seen in NF1.

Allelic heterogeneity
Allelic heterogeneity refers to different mutations within the same gene causing similar clinical conditions. While allelic heterogeneity may contribute to phenotypic variability in some disorders, in this case, the siblings share the same NF1 mutation, so it does not account for the varying severities observed.

Germline mosaicism
Germline mosaicism occurs when a mutation is present in a subset of germ cells, potentially leading to offspring with genetic conditions despite unaffected parents. Here, both siblings inherited the same mutation from their parents, making germline mosaicism an unlikely explanation for their differing symptoms.

Penetrance
Penetrance describes the proportion of individuals with a genotype who express the associated phenotype. Both siblings exhibit features of neurofibromatosis type 1, indicating full penetrance, but this does not explain the variability in severity, which is due to expressivity.

Variable inheritance
Variable inheritance suggests differences in the pattern of inheritance, such as autosomal dominant versus recessive. However, neurofibromatosis type 1 follows a clear autosomal dominant inheritance, so this term does not apply.

stem: You have collected data as part of a study into a new suture being used as part of a hysterectomy. In the study, patients are randomised into 2 groups. One group receives a newly developed suture, and the other receives the usual suture. The main outcome measure is the length of hospital stay. Initial analysis of the data reveals that the lengths of stay in the intervention group are positively skewed and do not follow a normal distribution. Which of the following statistical tests should be used to compare whether the average length of hospital stay differed between the two groups?
explanation:
Mann-Whitney U test
Mann-Whitney U test is the most appropriate test to use in this scenario, as the data is not paired, and is not normally distributed. This test compares the differences between two independent groups of ordinal or interval data when the assumption of a normal distribution cannot be justified, and parametric testing such as a t-test cannot be used.

Paired sample t-test
Paired sample t-test is incorrect; the data is not paired in this scenario, and this is a parametric test, used on normally distributed data.

Independent sample t-test
Independent sample t-test is incorrect; this would be used if the data were approximately normally distributed.

Wilcoxon signed-rank test
Wilcoxon signed-rank test is incorrect; this is a non-parametric test that can be used for data that is not normally distributed as in this case. However, it is used when data is paired, which is not the case in this scenario.

One-way analysis of variance analysis (ANOVA)
One-way ANOVA is incorrect; this is used for parametric/approximately normally distributed data, when the mean needs to be compared for more than 2 groups.

stem: A 30-year-old woman is referred to the rheumatologist with a one-week history of persistent right knee pain, sore eyes, and swelling as well as lower back stiffness. She feels otherwise generally well and is on the seventh day of a course of ciprofloxacin for a suspected UTI. Four weeks ago, she was treated at the sexual health clinic for Chlamydia and gonococcus co-infection. Blood tests show: Hb 132 g/L (115 - 160) WBC 10.4 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) CRP 55 mg/L (< 5) On examination, her right knee and right ankle are noted to be swollen and tender. Given the likely diagnosis, what HLA serotype is this condition associated with?
explanation:
HLA-B27
Reactive arthritis would best fit this presentation. Associated with HLA-B27, this typically presents with arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis. This woman clearly has acute onset arthritis and is being treated for a 'suspected UTI' which has not resolved after the usual three days of treatment that would be used to treat women and which should raise suspicion of urethritis. She describes the probable trigger for her reactive arthritis- Chlamydia infection.

HLA-B51
HLA-B51 is associated with Behcet's disease, which usually presents with ulcers of the genitals and oral mucosa, skin lesions, and inflammation of parts of the eye.

HLA-DQ2
HLA-DQ2 is associated with Coeliac disease, which would present with symptoms of malabsorption.

HLA-DR3
