HLA-DR3 is associated with Addison's disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, type 1 diabetes mellitus, Grave's disease, and myasthenia gravis. None of these would give the presentation above.

HLA-DR4
HLA-DR4 is associated with type 1 diabetes mellitus and rheumatoid arthritis.

stem: Which foramen does the maxillary nerve go through?
explanation:
Foramen rotundum
The maxillary nerve (V2) passes through the foramen rotundum, making this the correct answer. This is an important anatomical relationship to understand as the maxillary nerve provides sensory innervation to the maxillary teeth, upper lip, cheek, and lower eyelid. The foramen rotundum is located in the base of the skull and serves as a dedicated passage for this branch of the trigeminal nerve.

Jugular foramen
Jugular foramen is incorrect as this foramen transmits the glossopharyngeal (CN IX), vagus (CN X) and accessory (CN XI) nerves, along with the internal jugular vein. It does not transmit any branches of the trigeminal nerve.

Foramen ovale
Foramen ovale is incorrect as this transmits the mandibular nerve (V3), which is a different branch of the trigeminal nerve. While related to the maxillary nerve as part of the trigeminal system, it has its own dedicated foramen.

Superior orbital fissure
Superior orbital fissure is incorrect as this transmits the ophthalmic nerve (V1), oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV) and abducens (VI) nerves into the orbit. While it transmits another branch of the trigeminal nerve, it is not the pathway for the maxillary nerve.

Optic canal
Optic canal is incorrect as this only transmits the optic nerve (CN II) and ophthalmic artery. It has no relationship with the maxillary nerve or other branches of the trigeminal nerve.

stem: You are called to review a 43-year-old man who was previously fit and well who has been stabbed in the back following an assault. A 3cm puncture wound is noted just to the right of the T5 vertebra. On examination, he has a loss of fine touch sensation on the right side. If present, where would you expect to find a loss of temperature sensation?
explanation:
Left side, below the lesion
The spinothalamic tract decussates at the same level the nerve root enters the spinal cord. The corticospinal tract, dorsal column medial lemniscus, and spinocerebellar tracts decussate at the medulla. The stimuli that need to be responded to quickly (pain and temperature) cross first. Brown-Sequard syndrome represents a clinical manifestation of the body's anatomical idiosyncrasies. To answer these questions, you must understand which types of nerve fibres decussate at the spinal level, and which decussate within the brain itself. Pain and temperature are carried in the spinothalamic tract which decussates at the spinal level it enters at. So a hemisection of the cord will result in contralateral loss of these functions. The puncture wound is on the right, so the contralateral loss would present on the left. It will be below the lesion as the fibres run in the caudocranial direction. Left side, below the lesion, is correct.

Left side, above the lesion
Left side, above the lesion, is incorrect, as the loss will always be below the lesion.

Right side, below the lesion
Right side, below the lesion, is incorrect as the loss will be contralateral. Fine touch, vibration, and proprioception loss would be found in this distribution, however.

Right side, above the lesion
Right side, above the lesion, is incorrect on two counts, for the reasons given above.

Bilaterally
The loss would be bilateral if there was a complete severing of the cord. This is not the case here.

stem: In the kidney, the loop of Henle is the portion of a nephron that leads from the proximal convoluted tubule to the distal convoluted tubule. By means of a countercurrent multiplier system, which uses electrolyte pumps, the loop of Henle creates an area of high urea concentration deep in the medulla. This results in the reabsorption of water and concentration of urine for excretion. The thin ascending limb of the loop of Henle is impermeable to what substance?
explanation:
Water
The thin ascending limb of the loop of Henle is impermeable to water. Water is correct. The thin ascending limb is impermeable to water, but highly permeable to sodium and chloride ions.

Chloride ions
Chloride ions is incorrect. The thick ascending limb is highly permeable to the reabsorption of sodium and chloride ions which occurs by both facilitated and passive diffusion pathways.

Magnesium ions
Magnesium ions is incorrect. The loop of Henle is the site of the majority of magnesium absorption from the kidneys. Approximately 60% to 70% of filtered magnesium is reabsorbed in the cortical thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.

Potassium ions
Potassium ions is incorrect. The medullary ascending limb is permeable to potassium ions.

Sodium ions
Sodium ions is incorrect. The medullary ascending limb is permeable to sodium ions.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with fatigue and pallor. Blood tests reveal the following: Hb 85 g/L Male: (135 - 180) Female: (115 - 160) LDH 420 U/L (120 - 250) Indirect bilirubin 37 µmol/L (0 - 17) On examination, heart sounds are normal. A stained peripheral blood smear shows erythrocytes containing a fine, mesh-like network. What does this finding indicate?
options: Abnormal haemoglobin aggregation in mature red cells
Fragmented red cells from mechanical hemolysis
Premature release of immature red cells with residual RNA
explanation:
Premature release of immature red cells with residual RNA
Reticulocytes have a mesh-like (reticular) network of ribosomal RNA that is visible when stained. This is not present in mature erythrocytes. Premature release of immature red cells with residual RNA is the correct answer. The mesh-like network seen represents residual ribosomal RNA present in reticulocytes. In a patient with anaemia, raised LDH and indirect hyperbilirubinaemia, there is likely haemolysis. An elevated reticulocyte count reflects a compensatory bone marrow response to this.

Abnormal haemoglobin aggregation in mature red cells
Abnormal haemoglobin aggregation in mature red cells is incorrect. Haemoglobin aggregation (e.g., in sickle cell disease) causes changes in red cell shape and deformability but does not produce the mesh-like RNA network visible on supravital staining. Mature erythrocytes lack RNA and would not show this pattern.

Artifact from staining procedure
Artifact from staining procedure is incorrect. While staining artefacts can occur, the consistent presence of mesh-like reticular structures in the context of hemolysis and anaemia is a true reflection of reticulocytes containing residual RNA, not an artefact.

Fragmented red cells from mechanical hemolysis
Fragmented red cells from mechanical hemolysis is incorrect. Schistocytes or fragmented red cells result from mechanical destruction and appear as irregular, jagged cells on a smear, but do not contain residual RNA. They lack the characteristic reticular staining seen in reticulocytes.

Membrane defects causing spherocytes
Membrane defects causing spherocytes is incorrect. Spherocytes are spherical red cells due to membrane loss, as seen in hereditary spherocytosis or autoimmune hemolytic anaemia. They do not contain residual RNA or show the mesh-like network on supravital stain.

stem: How is the left ventricular ejection fraction calculated?
options: End systolic LV volume / end diastolic LV volume
End diastolic LV volume / end systolic LV volume
End diastolic LV volume / stroke volume
End systolic LV volume - end diastolic LV volume
Stroke volume / end diastolic LV volume
explanation:
Stroke volume / end diastolic LV volume
The correct answer is Stroke volume / end diastolic LV volume. Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) is a key measure of cardiac function that represents the percentage of blood ejected from the left ventricle during systole relative to the total volume of blood in the ventricle at the end of diastole. The formula for calculating LVEF is: LVEF = (Stroke Volume / End Diastolic Volume) × 100%. Where stroke volume is the difference between end diastolic volume and end systolic volume. Stroke volume / end diastolic LV volume is the correct formula for calculating LVEF. This ratio represents the fraction of blood that is ejected during systole compared to the total amount of blood in the ventricle before contraction. Normal LVEF values typically range from 55-70%, with values below 40% generally indicating significant cardiac dysfunction.

End systolic LV volume / end diastolic LV volume
End systolic LV volume / end diastolic LV volume is incorrect. This formula actually calculates the residual fraction, which is the proportion of blood remaining in the ventricle after systole. This is the opposite of what we want to measure with LVEF.

End diastolic LV volume / end systolic LV volume
End diastolic LV volume / end systolic LV volume is incorrect. This formula does not represent any standard cardiac parameter and would yield values greater than 1 in normal hearts, which does not align with the concept of ejection fraction as a percentage of blood ejected.

End diastolic LV volume / stroke volume
End diastolic LV volume / stroke volume is incorrect. This formula represents the reciprocal of the ratio of stroke volume to end diastolic volume, which would give a value that is the inverse of the ejection fraction.

End systolic LV volume - end diastolic LV volume
End systolic LV volume - end diastolic LV volume is incorrect. This calculation would yield a negative value, as end systolic volume is always less than end diastolic volume in a functioning heart. Additionally, this formula calculates a volume difference rather than a ratio or percentage, which is not consistent with the definition of ejection fraction.

stem: Which one of the following is involved in the degradation of polypeptides?
explanation:
Proteasome
The correct answer is the Proteasome. Proteasomes are complex protein structures found in both the nucleus and cytoplasm of cells. They play a crucial role in the degradation of intracellular proteins, including polypeptides. This process involves breaking down the peptide bonds that hold the amino acids together in polypeptide chains, thereby degrading them into smaller peptides and individual amino acids. This mechanism is essential for maintaining cellular homeostasis by removing damaged or misfolded proteins and regulating protein levels.

Peroxisome
The Peroxisome is not involved in polypeptide degradation but rather handles oxidative reactions within the cell. It contains enzymes that catalyse various metabolic processes such as fatty acid oxidation, cholesterol biosynthesis and bile acid production. Peroxisomes also play a role in detoxifying harmful substances like alcohol.

Endoplasmic reticulum
The Endoplasmic reticulum (ER), while an essential part of protein synthesis, does not degrade polypeptides. The rough ER has ribosomes on its surface where protein synthesis occurs, while smooth ER plays a vital role in lipid metabolism and detoxification processes.

Ribosome
The Ribosome is involved in protein synthesis rather than degradation. It translates mRNA into a polypeptide chain during translation, which is part of the process of gene expression.

Golgi apparatus
The Golgi apparatus functions mainly to modify, sort and package macromolecules for secretion or transport to other parts of the cell. However, it does not have any known function related to polypeptide degradation.

stem: A 23-year-old man is referred to the ophthalmologists with visual problems which are found to be caused by a downward dislocation of the lens in his right eye. The ophthalmologist notices his marfanoid habitus and history of learning disabilities. A diagnosis of homocystinuria is suspected. What is the pathophysiology of this condition?
explanation:
Deficiency of cystathionine beta synthase
Homocystinuria is caused by a deficiency of cystathionine beta synthase

Excess of cystathionine beta synthase
Interestingly, patients with Down's syndrome have an excess of cystathionine beta synthase.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a recurrent fever. He has a past medical history of Adult-onset Still's disease. During the course of the admission, the patient becomes more unwell, with high-grade fevers and tachycardia. Blood results are as follows: Hb 110 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) Platelets 82 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 2.1 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) CRP 74 mg/L (< 5) Ferritin 22,180 mg/mL (30-400) Triglycerides 4.8 mmol/L (<1.7) Fibrinogen 0.9 g/L (2 - 4) Given the likely diagnosis, what cytokine plays a key role in the pathophysiology?
explanation:
Interferon-γ
Interferon-γ is responsible for activating macrophages and plays a key role in the pathogenesis of macrophage activation syndrome. The patient has a diagnosis of Adult-onset Still's disease. In addition, the extremely high ferritin, cytopaenias, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypofibrinogenaemia are suggestive of macrophage activation syndrome which is a severe, potentially life-threatening, complication of several chronic rheumatological diseases.

IL-2
IL-2 acts on Th1 cells to stimulate the growth and differentiation of T cell response.

IL-3
IL-3 acts on activated T helper cells to stimulate differentiation and proliferation of myeloid progenitor cells.

IL-4
IL-4 acts on Th2 cells to stimulate proliferation and differentiation of B cells.

IL-5
IL-5 acts on Th2 cells to stimulate production of eosinophils.

stem: Where is the majority of iron found in the body?
explanation:
Haemoglobin
The correct answer is haemoglobin, which contains approximately 60-70% of total body iron. Iron is an essential component of haemoglobin, where it forms part of the haem molecule that allows oxygen binding and transport throughout the body. Each haemoglobin molecule contains four haem groups, with each haem containing one iron atom.

Bone
Bone contains relatively little iron. While bone marrow is the site of erythropoiesis and therefore iron utilization, the bone tissue itself does not store significant amounts of iron.

Ferritin and haemosiderin
Ferritin and haemosiderin are iron storage proteins that together contain about 25-30% of total body iron. While this is a significant proportion, it is still less than that found in haemoglobin. These proteins are particularly concentrated in the liver, spleen and bone marrow.

Myoglobin
Myoglobin contains only about 3-4% of total body iron. While myoglobin is important for oxygen storage in muscle tissue, the total amount of iron contained within myoglobin is much less than that in haemoglobin.

Plasma iron
Plasma iron represents less than 1% of total body iron. This iron is bound to transferrin for transport between sites of absorption, storage and utilization. The small amount reflects the efficient uptake and storage of iron by tissues.

stem: Which of the following is responsible for the early repolarisation phase of the myocardial action potential?
explanation:
Efflux of potassium
The correct answer is the efflux of potassium. The early repolarisation phase of the myocardial action potential, also known as phase 1, is primarily driven by the efflux (outward flow) of potassium ions. At this stage, there's a rapid outflow of potassium ions from the intracellular to the extracellular space which causes a brief period of repolarisation after the initial depolarisation spike.

Rapid sodium influx
Rapid sodium influx is responsible for the initial rapid depolarisation phase (phase 0) of the action potential. This occurs when voltage-gated sodium channels open in response to a stimulus, allowing sodium ions to rush into the cell and causing a rapid change in membrane potential from negative to positive.

Rapid calcium influx
Rapid calcium influx is associated with the plateau phase (phase 2) of the action potential. During this phase, slow voltage-gated calcium channels open allowing an influx of calcium ions into the cell. This balances out with continued potassium efflux resulting in a prolonged depolarised state or 'plateau' which distinguishes cardiac muscle cells from nerve and skeletal muscle cells.

Slow sodium efflux
Slow sodium efflux does not play a significant role in any specific phase of myocardial action potential. Sodium efflux mainly occurs via active transport using ATPase pumps during the resting state to maintain electrochemical gradients rather than during specific phases of action potentials.

Slow efflux of calcium
The option slow efflux of calcium is also incorrect because it doesn't contribute significantly to early repolarisation. Instead, slow efflux or removal of calcium ions occurs during the late repolarisation phase (phase 3), alongside continued potassium efflux, contributing towards returning membrane potential back to its resting state.

stem: A 17-year-old boy presents with a 12 hour history of seizures and acute confusion, with a chronic history of headaches. There is a strong family history of cancers occurring prior to the age of 45. An MRI head displays a high-density space-occupying lesion. He undergoes craniotomy and resection. Histology later reveals a high-grade glioma. A whole-body MRI reveals: Small diaphyseal osteosarcoma of the distal tibia. What gene mutation is likely to be responsible for this presentation?
explanation:
TP53
p53 - plays a crucial role in the cell cycle, preventing entry into the S phase until DNA has been checked and repaired. This scenario is describing a case of Li Fraumeni syndrome, a rare autosomal dominant condition that is characterised by multiple early onset primary malignancies. It occurs due to germline mutations in TP53. TP53 is a tumour suppressor gene that encodes tumour protein P53, which plays a key role in DNA repair and preventing DNA damage. It regulates the checkpoint following the G1 phase of the cell cycle, also known as the G1/S transition.

The G1 phase is where the cell grows and produces the protein and mRNA required for DNA synthesis. Prior to entering S phase, where DNA is replicated, the cell must progress through regulated checkpoints that prevent the synthesis of damaged DNA that has the potential to repress apoptosis and proliferate without regulation. p53 can regulate this by both arresting cell cycle progression as well as initiating DNA repair and inducing apoptosis. Mutations in p53 result in an inactive form of the protein, which can lead to deranged apoptosis and ultimately uncontrolled cell proliferation and cancer formation. The typical features of Li Fraumeni syndrome include early-onset (<45 years) osteosarcomas, breast cancers, brain cancers, soft tissue sarcomas and adrenal carcinomas, with a similar history in first degree relatives. Regular whole-body imaging and ultrasound/biochemical screening are advised.

APC
APC is implicated in many cell functions, chiefly, cytoskeletal regulation and control of cell polarity. Mutations in APC are implicated in familial adenomatous polyposis, which is strongly associated with colorectal cancer. Patients would typically present with a change in bowel habit and a strong family history of colorectal cancer, unlike what is described here.

BRCA1
BRCA1 is responsible for the repair of DNA double-strand breaks. Mutations in this gene result in error-prone DNA repair and can cause breast and ovarian cancers. BRCA1 mutations are responsible for ~35% of all hereditary breast cancers. Patients would not be pre-disposed to gliomas or osteosarcomas as described here.

MLH1
MLH1 encodes a protein responsible for DNA mismatch repair. Mutations are associated with hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC). HNPCC typically presents with early-onset colorectal and/or endometrial cancer. This is not described here.

NF1
NF1 encodes a protein called neurofibromin, which negatively regulates the RAS pathway - a process that promotes cell division and survival. Mutations are associated with neurofibromatosis type 1, whereby patients can exhibit cafe au lait spots, neurofibromas, optic gliomas and Lisch nodules. This is not described here.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents with acute, painless bilateral vision loss over 2 weeks. He reports a central scotoma but no eye pain. His mother and a maternal uncle experienced similar acute visual loss in early adulthood. Fundoscopy reveals temporal pallor of the optic discs. Genetic testing is planned. Which inheritance pattern is most likely responsible for this condition?
explanation:
Mitochondrial
Leber's Hereditary Optic Neuropathy: mitochondrial inheritance pattern Mitochondrial is correct, as Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) is caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA, which is inherited exclusively maternally. This patient’s presentation with acute bilateral vision loss in a young male with a family history of similar symptoms is classic for LHON. Mitochondrial inheritance explains why the condition is transmitted through the mother (as sperm do not contribute mitochondria to the zygote) and why males are more frequently affected, despite the non-X-linked pattern.

Autosomal dominant
Autosomal dominant is incorrect, as autosomal dominant conditions (e.g., Huntington’s disease) affect both sexes equally and typically show male-to-male transmission, which is absent here.

Autosomal recessive
Autosomal recessive is incorrect, as autosomal recessive disorders (e.g., cystic fibrosis) require mutations in both alleles, usually with unaffected parents. The pattern of inheritance suggested by multiple affected relatives across generations makes this unlikely.

X-linked dominant
X-linked dominant is incorrect, as X-linked dominant conditions (e.g., fragile X syndrome) rarely affect males more severely, as males inherit only one X chromosome. LHON’s male predominance is unrelated to Xlinked mechanisms.

X-linked recessive
X-linked recessive is incorrect, as X-linked recessive disorders (e.g., Duchenne muscular dystrophy) predominantly affect males, but carrier females are usually asymptomatic. Here, the presence of affected individuals across generations without a male-limited pattern makes Xlinked recessive inheritance unlikely.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with a symmetrical arthropathy affecting her hands. On examination she has synovitis of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpophalangeal joints. What type of HLA allele is most associated with this condition?
explanation:
HLA DR4
Rheumatoid arthritis - HLA DR4 This patient has rheumatoid arthritis.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents for routine antenatal screening at 12 weeks' gestation. Ultrasound findings reveal a nuchal translucency of 3.2 mm and a flat nasal bridge. There is no significant family history of genetic disorders. Combined screening shows an elevated risk for a chromosomal abnormality. A follow-up test, chorionic villus sampling, is suggested to confirm the findings. Based on the findings, what neurodegenerative disease is this child at increased risk of developing later in life?
explanation:
Alzheimer’s disease
Alzheimer’s disease is correct. The findings outlined in this scenario are suggestive of Down syndrome, also known as trisomy 21, given the ultrasound findings of increased nuchal translucency and a flat nasal bridge, which are supportive markers. Additionally, the combined screening identifying an elevated risk of a chromosomal abnormality further supports this. Individuals with Down syndrome are at a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. It is thought that the extra copy of chromosome 21 leads to an overproduction of amyloid precursor protein, which contributes to the development of amyloid plaques, a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease. These plaques, along with tau tangles, accumulate in the brain, leading to the early onset of Alzheimer’s disease in this population.

Huntington’s disease
Huntington’s disease is incorrect because it is a genetic disorder caused by a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene on chromosome 4, producing mutant huntingtin proteins, causing neurodegeneration. Huntington’s disease is not associated with the chromosomal abnormalities found in Down syndrome.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is incorrect because MS is an autoimmune condition that affects the central nervous system, leading to inflammation and damage to myelin. MS is not associated with Down syndrome and does not result from chromosomal abnormalities.

Parkinson’s disease
Parkinson’s disease is incorrect because Parkinson’s disease is a neurodegenerative disorder primarily affecting motor function, caused by a loss of dopamine-producing cells in the substantia nigra of the brain. It is not associated with Down syndrome.

Wilson’s disease
Wilson’s disease is incorrect because Wilson’s disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, leading to copper accumulation primarily in the liver and brain. It is not associated with Down syndrome.

stem: An 18-year-old man is seen in the infectious diseases clinic some 6 weeks after admission to the Emergency department with meningococcal meningitis. This was confirmed on lumbar puncture and represented his second episode of meningitis over the last 6 months. He has no other past medical history and takes no regular medication. Which of the following is most likely to be deficient?
explanation:
C5
C5 is cleaved into C5a and C5b, C5a is involved in chemotaxis, and C5b forms the first part of the membrane attack complex. Deficiencies of the membrane attack complex, (C5-C9) are particularly associated with meningococcal infection. C5 activation may also have a role in progression of fibrotic liver disease.

C1
Deficiencies of the C1 complex are recognised to be closely associated with the development of systemic lupus erythematosus.

C3
C3 deficiency is associated with a predisposition to infection with capsulated bacterial infections such as pneumococcus and Haemophilus which begins quite soon after birth.

C4
C4 deficiency is rare and is associated with early onset systemic lupus erythematosus.

CD59
CD59 deficiency is involved in the pathogenesis of paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents for medical assessment with reports of three months of joint pains that are worse in the morning. He has no past medical history. On examination, all distal interphalangeal joints (DIPJs) are symmetrically swollen, red, and tender on both hands. Given the likely diagnosis, what is the probable HLA association?
explanation:
HLA-B27
Psoriatic arthritis is associated with HLA B27. HLA-B27 is correct. The patient presents with joint pains that are worse in the morning, suggesting an inflammatory cause. The examination reveals symmetrical DIPJ swelling. Psoriatic arthritis is the most likely inflammatory arthritis to cause DIPJ-predominant inflammatory joint disease.

HLA-A3
HLA-A3 is incorrect. This is the HLA association for hemochromatosis. This can cause arthritis but involves the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints rather than the DIPJs when it affects the hands.

HLA-B51
HLA-B51 is incorrect. This is the HLA association for Behcet's syndrome. This can cause arthritis but again if it affects the hands it tends to be the MCPJs and PIPJs rather than the DIPJs. Additionally, the absence of oral and genital ulceration makes this diagnosis extremely unlikely.

HLA-DQ2
HLA-DQ2 is incorrect. This is the HLA association for coeliac disease. This can cause arthritis or arthralgia. However, it tends to be larger joints that are affected i.e. knees, ankles rather than hands so this is not likely.

HLA-DR4
HLA-DR4 is incorrect. This is the HLA association for rheumatoid arthritis. This disorder tends to spare the DIPJs and so this is incorrect.

stem: A 15-year-old girl presents with an urticarial rash, angioedema and wheezing. Her mother states that she has just come from her younger sister's party where she had been helping to blow up balloons. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Latex allergy
The correct answer is latex allergy. This patient's presentation is highly suggestive of a type I hypersensitivity reaction to latex exposure from handling balloons. The combination of urticaria, angioedema, and bronchospasm (wheezing) represents a classic allergic response mediated by IgE antibodies. Latex allergy is particularly common in healthcare workers and individuals with frequent exposure to latex products, and latex balloons are a well-known trigger.

C1-esterase deficiency (hereditary angioedema)
C1-esterase deficiency (hereditary angioedema) typically presents with recurrent episodes of non-pruritic angioedema without urticaria. Unlike this case, it is not triggered by latex exposure and is not associated with wheezing. It is an inherited condition caused by deficiency or dysfunction of C1 inhibitor protein.

Allergic contact dermatitis
Allergic contact dermatitis is a type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction that typically develops 24-48 hours after exposure to an allergen. It presents with erythema, vesicles, and pruritus but does not cause immediate angioedema or respiratory symptoms. Common triggers include nickel, fragrances, and topical medications.

Peanut allergy
Peanut allergy, while capable of causing similar symptoms through a type I hypersensitivity reaction, is not relevant in this scenario as there is no history of peanut exposure. The temporal relationship with balloon inflation strongly points towards latex as the allergen.

Irritant contact dermatitis
Irritant contact dermatitis is a non-immunological reaction caused by direct damage to the skin from exposure to irritants. It does not cause systemic symptoms such as angioedema or wheezing, and symptoms are typically confined to the area of contact. It presents with burning, stinging, and erythema rather than urticaria.

stem: An asylum-seeker is rescued from a boat and brought to the emergency department for medical attention. An accompanying friend confirms the patient has had very little intake over the past months, eating mainly maize. She reports the patient has been suffering from progressive weakness, diarrhoea and a deterioration in her memory. On exam, she appears wasted with red, inflamed skin, especial of the sun-exposed areas and has a consistent cognitive deficit with poor memory, social interaction, and speech variation. What vitamin deficiency is the most likely cause for this patient's condition?
explanation:
Vitamin B3
Pellagra is caused by vitamin B3 (niacin) deficiency. This patient has presented with symptoms in keeping with pellagra, a condition secondary to vitamin B3 (niacin) deficiency. The classic triad of presentation is diarrhoea, dermatitis (especially in sun-exposed areas) and dementia. Pellagra can result from poor nutritional intake, particularly in patients who mainly consume the staple food maize as this is very low in absorbable vitamin B3. The amino acid tryptophan is also required for the body to make use of vitamin B3 and therefore tryptophan deficiency can also cause pellagra. It can therefore be secondary to other conditions which alter protein metabolism and deplete tryptophan stores such as carcinoid syndrome.

Vitamin A
Vitamin A deficiency is normally due to poor dietary intake and is mainly associated with visual issues. Night blindness is the earliest feature of vitamin A deficiency which can progress to complete blindness without intervention. Vitamin A plays a major role in phototransduction, and its deficiency reduces the production of the photopigment rhodopsin, responsible for low light vision. Vitamin A deficiency can also cause a general reduction in immunity but is not normally associated with the non-ocular issues described in this case.

Vitamin B1
Vitamin B1, also known as thiamine, deficiency is responsible for beriberi disease which can affect the cardiovascular and/or the nervous system. Thiamine is required for the metabolism and production of several molecules within the body. Wet beriberi is associated with cardiac failure whereas dry beriberi results in peripheral neuropathies and encephalopathies (Wernicke's encephalopathy and Korsakoff syndrome). Although thiamine deficiency can cause several signs and symptoms, diarrhoea and dermatitis are not normally associated with the condition and encephalopathy is more commonly seen instead of dementia.

Vitamin B12
Vitamin B12 deficiency can result from poor dietary intake or absorption dysfunction such as in the condition pernicious anaemia where patients lack intrinsic factor (required to absorb vitamin B12). It is most commonly associated with causing macrocytic anaemia, as vitamin B12 is required to synthesise new red blood cells. Again, skin issues and diarrhoea are not traditionally associated with vitamin B12 deficiency.

Vitamin C
Vitamin C deficiency results in the condition scurvy. Scurvy is classically associated with issues of the 4 Hs: haemorrhage (i.e., bleeding gums), hyperkeratosis (skin thickening), hypochondriasis (anxiety and other mental health illness), and haematologic abnormalities (i.e., anaemia & coagulopathies). Dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia are not typically associated with the condition.

stem: A 50-year-old man with multiple cardiac risk factors presents to the hospital with acute onset central chest pain. The pain radiates to his left arm and is associated with nausea and sweating. His ECG shows widespread T-wave inversion, which is new when compared to his previous ECGs. The serum level of troponin I is measured and confirmed to be raised. The patient is started on acute coronary syndrome treatment and transferred to a cardiac centre. What does this measured cardiac biomarker bind to?
explanation:
Actin
Troponin I binds to actin to hold the troponin-tropomyosin complex in place. Actin holds the troponin-tropomyosin complex in place which regulates muscle contraction. Troponin I is one of three subunits of troponin and is released in myocardial damage; it is generally considered to be more sensitive and significantly more specific in the diagnosis of myocardial infarction than other cardiac biomarkers.

Calcium ions
Calcium ions are bound to by troponin C, playing the main role in Ca2+ dependent regulation of muscle contraction. Troponin C is another of the three subunits of troponin and as such can be used in the diagnosis of myocardial infarction; however, as troponin C is found in both cardiac and skeletal muscle (unlike troponin I and T), it is less specific.

Copeptin
Copeptin is an amino acid peptide that is made in the hypothalamus and stored in the posterior pituitary. Research has shown that copeptin is released much earlier than troponin during the onset of acute myocardial infarction, raising the potential for diagnostic use. It is not currently widely used in clinical practice and has no interaction with troponin.

Myoglobin
Myoglobin is an iron- and oxygen-binding protein found in both the cardiac and skeletal muscle, similar in structure to haemoglobin. Raised myoglobin levels can be found following acute myocardial infarction, but it has poor specificity for cardiac injury. It is not involved in the troponin-tropomyosin complex.

Sodium ions
Sodium ions are involved in voltage-gated channels found on cell plasma membranes throughout the body. Although part of the electrical cardiac conduction system, sodium ions are not involved in the troponin-tropomyosin complex and play no role in cardiac biomarkers.

stem: A study is being conducted, examining a novel blood test that aims to detect the presence of a pulmonary embolism (PE). It is being compared against the gold-standard - CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) scanning. 200 patients are recruited to the study from a respiratory ward, over time. 80 of these patients have demonstrable PE on CTPA, and 120 do not. Of the 80 with PE, 60 have a positive new blood test result. Of the 120 without PE, 15 have a positive blood test result. What is the positive predictive value of the new blood test?
explanation:
0.8
Positive predictive value (PPV) refers to the chance that the patient has the condition if the diagnostic test in question is positive. With regards to this test, there are (60 + 15) = 75 positive blood test results. Of these 75 patients, 60 actually have PE as demonstrated by CTPA. As such, the PPV is (60 / 75) = 0.8.

0.6
The value of 0.6 is not meaningful with respect to this scenario.

0.75
The sensitivity of this test is 0.75. This is the proportion of patients with the condition (80, as detected by CTPA) who have a positive test result (60).

0.84
The negative predictive value of this test is 0.84. This refers to the chance that the patient does not have the condition if the test is negative. In this case, the total number of negative tests is (20 + 105) = 125. Out of these, 105 do not have the condition (according to CTPA results) and so (105 / 125) = 0.84.

0.88
The specificity of this test is 0.88. This refers to the proportion of patients without the condition (120) who have a negative test result (105).

stem: You have been asked to prepare a presentation for the hospital journal club on a novel drug in the treatment of heart failure. You find a relevant recent systematic review and meta-analysis which combines data from multiple randomised controlled trials investigating the effectiveness of the novel drug on five-year survival in patients with heart failure. A figure in the meta-analysis shows each study as a dot on a plot where the x-axis represents the odds ratio for each study and the y-axis is the standard error of the odds ratio for each study. What is the name of figure?
explanation:
Funnel plot
Funnel plots - show publication bias in meta-analyses The plot described is a funnel plot which is used to visually assess for publication bias in meta-analysis. Publication bias can result from differences in the chances of a study being published based on the findings of that study; typically, it stems from the relative underrepresentation in the literature of studies with non-significant results. A funnel plot is a scatter-plot where each study is plotted as a point. The x-axis is some measure of effect size (in this case odds ratio) and the y-axis is some measure of precision (in this case standard error of the odds ratio). The idea is that if there is no publication bias, larger studies with more precise results will cluster around the top of the plot, with smaller studies spreading out symmetrically below them (to create a sort of triangle shape/upside down funnel shape). The key is the symmetry of the plot: you expect as many smaller studies with results less extreme than the larger studies as smaller studies with results more extreme.

Box plot
A box plot is a commonly used plot to visually display the distribution and skew of data from a single study or experiment. It is not typically used in meta-analysis.

Forest plot
A forest plot is another commonly used plot in meta-analysis and is a way to visualise results from multiple studies. Like funnel plots, forest plots also use effect size (e.g. odds ratio) on the x-axis. However, there is no formal y-axis. In place of a y-axis, there is a vertical line which represents the line of no effect. Each study is plotted as a box on a horizontal line above the x-axis; the position of the box along the x-axis is the estimated effect size for that study and the line spans the 95% confidence intervals for the estimate. A diamond is typically plotted at the bottom of the forest plot which shows the average effect size from all studies.

Kaplan-Meir curve
A Kaplan-Meir curve is a visual display of a survival function, which shows the probability of an event at a given time. It therefore has some measure of probability (usually survival) on the y-axis and a measure of time on the x-axis.

Manhattan plot
A Manhattan plot is used to display data from genome-wide association studies. It has the chromosomal position of a genetic locus on the x-axis, and the significance of the association of that locus with the disease on the y-axis.

stem: Which one of the following is only secreted by the adrenal medulla?
explanation:
Adrenaline
The correct answer is Adrenaline. Adrenaline, also known as epinephrine, is a hormone that is only secreted by the adrenal medulla. It plays an essential role in the body's response to stress, increasing heart rate, blood pressure and metabolic rate. In addition, it enhances muscle strength and mental alertness.

Noradrenaline
Noradrenaline, also known as norepinephrine, is not exclusively secreted by the adrenal medulla. While it is indeed produced in the adrenal medulla, it is also synthesized in nerve terminals of the sympathetic nervous system. Noradrenaline acts as both a hormone and a neurotransmitter playing a crucial role in maintaining blood pressure and supporting the fight-or-flight response.

Aldosterone
Aldosterone is incorrect because it is not secreted by the adrenal medulla but rather by the adrenal cortex. Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid hormone that regulates sodium and potassium balance in the body and thus helps to control blood volume and pressure.

Metadrenaline
Metadrenaline, or metanephrine, are metabolites of adrenaline and noradrenaline but they themselves are not directly secreted by the adrenal glands. They are typically measured in urine tests for pheochromocytoma, which are rare tumours that release excessive amounts of adrenaline and noradrenaline.

Cortisol
Cortisol is also not secreted by the adrenal medulla but by the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex. Cortisol is a glucocorticoid hormone that plays important roles in glucose metabolism, immune function regulation, and stress response among several other functions.

stem: Which one of the following statements is true regarding interferon?
options: Interferon-alpha and interferon-beta bind to the same type of receptor
Interferon-gamma has stronger antiviral action than interferon-alpha
Interferon-alpha has been shown to reduce the frequency of exacerbations in patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis
Interferon-gamma has a role in chronic hepatitis C
explanation:
Interferon-alpha and interferon-beta bind to the same type of receptor
Interferon-alpha and interferon-beta bind to the same type of receptor is the correct answer. Interferons are classified into three main types: Type I (which includes interferon-alpha and interferon-beta), Type II (interferon-gamma), and Type III (interferon-lambda). Interferon-alpha and interferon-beta both bind to the Type I interferon receptor (IFNAR), which consists of two subunits: IFNAR1 and IFNAR2. This shared receptor binding explains why these two interferons have overlapping biological activities, particularly in antiviral responses. Upon binding to their receptor, they activate the JAK-STAT signalling pathway, leading to the transcription of interferon-stimulated genes that mediate their biological effects.

Interferon-beta is produced by leucocytes
Interferon-beta is produced by leucocytes is incorrect. Interferon-beta is primarily produced by fibroblasts and epithelial cells, not leucocytes. In contrast, interferon-alpha is mainly produced by leucocytes, particularly plasmacytoid dendritic cells. This distinction in cellular sources is important for understanding the different contexts in which these interferons are produced during immune responses.

Interferon-gamma has stronger antiviral action than interferon-alpha
Interferon-gamma has stronger antiviral action than interferon-alpha is incorrect. Interferon-alpha actually has stronger direct antiviral activity compared to interferon-gamma. Type I interferons (alpha and beta) are the primary interferons involved in the immediate antiviral response. While interferon-gamma does have some antiviral properties, its main role is in immunomodulation, particularly in activating macrophages and enhancing cell-mediated immunity. Interferon-gamma is more important for responses against intracellular bacteria and parasites rather than viruses.

Interferon-alpha has been shown to reduce the frequency of exacerbations in patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis
Interferon-alpha has been shown to reduce the frequency of exacerbations in patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis is incorrect. It is interferon-beta, not interferon-alpha, that is used in the treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. Interferon-beta preparations (such as Avonex, Rebif, and Betaferon) have been shown in clinical trials to reduce the frequency of relapses and slow the progression of disability in multiple sclerosis. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) in the UK recommends interferon-beta as a disease-modifying therapy for suitable patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis.

Interferon-gamma has a role in chronic hepatitis C
Interferon-gamma has a role in chronic hepatitis C is incorrect. Interferon-alpha (not gamma) was historically a cornerstone in the treatment of chronic hepatitis C, often used in combination with ribavirin. Interferon-gamma has no established therapeutic role in hepatitis C treatment. It's worth noting that in current UK practice, direct-acting antivirals have largely replaced interferon-based regimens for hepatitis C due to their superior efficacy and more favourable side effect profile.

stem: Which of the following is not a tumour suppressor gene?
explanation:
myc
myc is an oncogene which encodes a transcription factor.

stem: A young boy is diagnosed as having DiGeorge syndrome. Which one of the following infections is he most at risk from, secondary to his immune system dysfunction?
explanation:
Cryptococcus neoformans
The correct answer is Cryptococcus neoformans. DiGeorge syndrome, also known as 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, is characterised by thymic hypoplasia or aplasia, leading to defective T-cell development and function. This T-cell deficiency particularly affects cell-mediated immunity, making patients highly susceptible to fungal infections, especially those caused by Cryptococcus neoformans. The organism is an opportunistic pathogen that typically causes severe infections in individuals with impaired T-cell immunity.

Klebsiella pneumoniae
Klebsiella pneumoniae is primarily associated with bacterial pneumonia and urinary tract infections. While immunocompromised patients may be at increased risk, defence against this organism relies more on innate immunity and antibody responses, which are relatively preserved in DiGeorge syndrome.

Haemophilus influenzae type b
Haemophilus influenzae type b infections are primarily prevented by antibody-mediated immunity. Patients with DiGeorge syndrome typically maintain adequate B-cell function and can produce antibodies, making this organism less of a specific threat compared to fungal pathogens.

Neisseria meningitidis
Neisseria meningitidis is primarily controlled by humoral immunity (antibodies) and complement, rather than T-cell-mediated immunity. While DiGeorge syndrome patients may have slightly increased susceptibility, this is not the organism they are most at risk from.

Salmonella typhi
Salmonella typhi, while potentially more severe in immunocompromised patients, is primarily controlled through a combination of innate immunity and antibody responses. The specific T-cell defect in DiGeorge syndrome does not particularly predispose to this infection compared to fungal infections.

stem: A 32-year-old woman is referred to the haematology clinic with persistent fatigue, night sweats, and weight loss for 3 months. Examination reveals cervical lymphadenopathy. A lymph node biopsy is performed, and the pathologist requests fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) to identify a specific chromosomal translocation. What is the most accurate description of this technique?
options: It detects RNA transcripts using gel electrophoresis and radioactive probes
It uses fluorescent DNA probes to bind to specific gene sequences for direct visualisation
It identifies protein products of oncogenes using enzyme-linked antibodies
It amplifies small segments of DNA through repeated cycles of denaturation and replication
It measures gene expression levels through quantification of mRNA
explanation:
It uses fluorescent DNA probes to bind to specific gene sequences for direct visualisation
Fluorescence in situ hybridization uses fluorescent DNA or RNA probes to bind to specific gene sites of interest for direct visualisation of chromosomal anomalies. It uses fluorescent DNA probes to bind to specific gene sequences for direct visualisation is the correct description of fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). In this patient's case, FISH would be particularly useful for identifying chromosomal translocations associated with lymphomas, such as t(14;18) in follicular lymphoma or t(11;14) in mantle cell lymphoma. FISH works by using fluorescently labelled DNA probes that are complementary to specific DNA sequences of interest. These probes hybridize (bind) to their target sequences in the patient's chromosomes, allowing direct visualisation of chromosomal abnormalities under a fluorescence microscope. This technique is valuable in haematological malignancies where specific genetic aberrations have diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic implications. FISH can detect translocations, deletions, amplifications, and other chromosomal rearrangements with high sensitivity.

It detects RNA transcripts using gel electrophoresis and radioactive probes
It detects RNA transcripts using gel electrophoresis and radioactive probes describes Northern blotting, not FISH. Northern blotting is used to detect specific RNA molecules in a sample. The RNA is separated by size using gel electrophoresis, transferred to a membrane, and then hybridized with labelled probes. While both techniques involve hybridization, Northern blotting detects RNA rather than DNA and typically uses a blotting process rather than in situ detection.

It identifies protein products of oncogenes using enzyme-linked antibodies
It identifies protein products of oncogenes using enzyme-linked antibodies describes techniques such as immunohistochemistry or Western blotting, not FISH. These protein detection methods use antibodies rather than nucleic acid probes. In the context of lymphoma diagnosis, immunohistochemistry would be used to identify cell surface markers or abnormal protein expression, but would not directly detect chromosomal abnormalities.

It amplifies small segments of DNA through repeated cycles of denaturation and replication
It amplifies small segments of DNA through repeated cycles of denaturation and replication describes polymerase chain reaction (PCR), not FISH. PCR is an amplification technique that creates multiple copies of a specific DNA segment, whereas FISH is a hybridization technique that visualizes DNA sequences in their chromosomal context without amplification.

It measures gene expression levels through quantification of mRNA
It measures gene expression levels through quantification of mRNA describes techniques such as real-time PCR or RNA sequencing, not FISH. These techniques quantify the amount of specific mRNA molecules to determine gene expression levels, whereas FISH localizes and visualizes specific DNA sequences within chromosomes.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the rheumatology clinic following a referral from his GP for joint pains. He has no significant past medical history but describes experiencing pain and stiffness in the small joints of his hands, along with lower back discomfort. His GP is concurrently investigating him for unexplained diarrhoea. During the physical examination, he exhibits tenderness over all distal interphalangeal joints, accompanied by nail pitting and onycholysis. What is most likely to be positive in this patient?
explanation:
HLA B27
Psoriatic arthritis is associated with HLA B27. The Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) system consists of antigen-presenting proteins encoded by a diverse set of genes. The various combinations of alleles lead to a broad spectrum of HLA types among individuals. Certain configurations within the HLA system can interact more robustly with the immune system, thereby mediating an inflammatory response. These responses may be autoimmune, thus establishing associations between certain HLA patterns and specific diseases. Considering the clinical presentation of arthritis in the distal interphalangeal joints (DIPJs), coupled with nail changes and lower back pain suggestive of potential sacroiliac involvement, this patient is most likely suffering from psoriatic arthritis. Psoriatic arthritis is associated with HLA B27, which can occur both with and without cutaneous manifestations typical of psoriasis.

HLA B51
HLA B51 has been linked to Behçet's disease, a form of vasculitis characterised by oral and genital ulcers, an increased risk for venous thromboembolism, and a rash. This condition has a strong correlation with smoking. This HLA marker is not as closely associated with psoriatic arthritis as HLA B27.

HLA DQ2
Coeliac disease, which causes gastrointestinal symptoms due to gluten intolerance, is associated with HLA DQ2, rather than HLA B27 which is not as closely associated.

HLA DR3
HLA DR3 is implicated in dermatitis herpetiformis - a pruritic papular rash frequently associated with coeliac disease - and Sjogren's syndrome, an autoimmune disorder targeting exocrine glands such as the lacrimal and salivary glands. It also plays a role in type 1 diabetes mellitus. Again, while HLA DR3 is associated with this autoimmune condition, it is not as closely related to psoriatic arthritis.

HLA DR4
HLA DR4 shows a stronger association with autoimmune type 1 diabetes mellitus and rheumatoid arthritis. However, this form of arthritis seldom affects the DIPJs as observed in this patient, nor does it typically result in the accompanying nail changes.

stem: A randomised controlled trial compares two drugs used in the initial management of rheumatoid arthritis. After being assigned to the randomised groups a number of patients drop out due to adverse effects of the medication. How should the data be analysed?
options: For each patient who drops out, remove a patient from the other randomised group
Include the patients who drop out in the final data set
Remove patients who drop out from final data set
Abandon the trial if more than 5% of patients drop out
explanation:
Include the patients who drop out in the final data set
The correct answer, in this case, is to include the patients who drop out in the final data set. This approach is known as intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis, which is a standard method for analysing randomised controlled trials. The main principle of ITT analysis is that all participants are analysed according to their original treatment allocation, regardless of whether they completed the intervention or not. This helps maintain the benefits of randomisation and provides a more conservative estimate of the treatment effect.

Recruit more patients
The option to recruit more patients may seem like a reasonable solution, but it does not address the issue of how to handle missing data from those who have already dropped out. Additionally, adding more patients could introduce bias if the new patients are not randomly allocated.

For each patient who drops out, remove a patient from the other randomised group
For each patient who drops out, remove a patient from the other randomised group would disrupt the balance achieved through randomisation and potentially introduce bias into the results. It also does not account for potential differences between those who drop out and those who remain in the study.

Remove patients who drop out from final data set
Removing patients who drop out from the final data set may lead to an overestimation of treatment effects by only including those with favourable outcomes. This approach is called per-protocol analysis and can be biased because it does not account for non-adherence or loss to follow-up.

Abandon the trial if more than 5% of patients drop out
Finally, abandoning the trial if more than 5% of patients drop out is an arbitrary threshold that may not be appropriate for all situations. Depending on the nature and severity of adverse effects, it might be important to continue investigating potential benefits or risks associated with these medications. Stopping a trial prematurely without sufficient evidence could lead to inconclusive results and wasted resources.

stem: You are a ST1 doctor in medicine. Whilst on-call you review a 60-year-old woman who is known to have COPD. She has been admitted with an infective exacerbation and has not responded to nebulisers and intravenous aminophylline. Her most recent blood gases show a worsening respiratory acidosis. You feel that non-invasive ventilation (NIV) is needed and bleep the on-call physio. After discussing the blood gas results over the phone she says that NIV is not indicated in her opinion and refuses to set it up. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Phone her back in 30 minutes and exaggerate the clinical picture
Accept her professional opinion and reassess the situation in 30 minutes
Set-up the NIV equipment yourself to avoid any further delay
As there is a disagreement on management speak to the consultant on-call
Transfer the patient to another hospital
explanation:
As there is a disagreement on management speak to the consultant on-call
By far the best option here is to speak to the consultant on-call. The physio may be experienced in providing NIV but it is ultimately a medical decision about whether to start a treatment.

Phone her back in 30 minutes and exaggerate the clinical picture
Lying about clinical information is a very poor option.

Accept her professional opinion and reassess the situation in 30 minutes
Accepting her opinion is a poor option as she has not reviewed the patient herself and is only giving an opinion on the basis of blood gases.

Set-up the NIV equipment yourself to avoid any further delay
Setting up NIV equipment requires training. If done incorrectly it could potentially harm a patient.

Transfer the patient to another hospital
Transferring an acutely unwell patient simply because the physio won't come in is not appropriate.

stem: A 78-year-old male patient who was admitted with a middle cerebral artery infarct that was complicated by a haemorrhagic transformation had a cardiac arrest on the medical ward. The team arrived and began chest compressions. The defibrillator showed the presence of sinus rhythm; there was no pulse was detected. The patient was given 1mg of intravenous medication in accordance with the Resuscitation Council UK adult advanced life support (ALS) algorithm and chest compressions were continued. What type of receptor does this drug act on?
explanation:
G protein-coupled receptors
Adrenaline acts via G protein-coupled receptors. Adrenaline binds to G protein-coupled receptors. G protein-coupled receptors, also known as seven-transmembrane domain receptors, are located in the cell membrane and bind to extracellular molecules and transmit signals intracellularly. When a ligand binds to the G-protein coupled receptor, it causes a conformational change in the receptor. This then causes an associated G protein to become activated by exchanging GDP for GTP. The two principal signalling pathways involved in G protein-coupled receptors intracellularly are cyclic AMP (cAMP) pathway and the phosphatidylinositol pathway.

Enzyme-linked receptors
Enzyme-linked receptors, or a catalytic receptor, is a transmembrane receptor, whereby the binding of an extracellular ligand results in enzymatic activity within the intracellular side. Examples include receptor tyrosine kinase.

Internal receptors
Internal receptors, or intracellular receptors, are in the cytoplasm of the cell and respond to hydrophobic ligand molecules that move across the plasma membrane. Examples include thyroid and steroid hormones.

Ion channel-linked receptors
Ion channel-linked receptors open in response to specific ligand molecules binding to the extracellular component of the receptor protein. An example of this type of receptor is acetylcholine receptors.

Voltage-sensitive ion channel
Voltage-sensitive ion channels are located in excitable tissues and are a potential target for drugs which block the channel or interfere with conductance in other ways. Example of ion channels which can be targeted include Na+ channels which are blocked by some local anaesthetics (e.g. lidocaine).

stem: A 42-year-old woman with class III obesity is enrolled in a clinical trial evaluating two novel pharmacological agents. One drug is designed to modulate leptin activity, and the other to influence ghrelin secretion. Early results show that stimulating one of these hormones reduces appetite and leads to weight loss. What is the most likely site of secretion of this hormone?
explanation:
Adipose tissue
Leptin is secreted by adipose tissue. Leptin is a hormone secreted primarily by adipose tissue in proportion to fat mass. In the scenario, appetite suppression and weight loss were observed following stimulation of a hormone that naturally reduces appetite — this corresponds to leptin. Leptin acts on the hypothalamus to inhibit hunger and promote energy expenditure. The patient's obesity implies leptin resistance, a common feature in individuals with high adiposity, which the drug may be aiming to overcome by enhancing leptin signalling. Therefore, the hormone responsible for this effect is secreted by adipose tissue.

Anterior pituitary
The anterior pituitary secretes several important hormones such as ACTH, TSH, GH, and prolactin, but it does not secrete either leptin or ghrelin. Its role in appetite regulation is indirect at best, primarily through modulation of metabolic hormones. In the context of the scenario, no drug targeting anterior pituitary hormones would account for the described effect on appetite. Including this option tests knowledge of neuroendocrine pathways, but it is not relevant to leptin or ghrelin secretion. Thus, this is an incorrect site in this clinical context.

Gastric fundus
The gastric fundus is the primary site of ghrelin secretion, which acts to stimulate appetite, not suppress it. In the scenario, the hormone that is being stimulated by the drug leads to reduced appetite, making ghrelin an unlikely candidate. This is a crucial detail, as it differentiates between the hormone effects being modulated. Thus, although ghrelin is relevant in obesity and acts on the hypothalamus like leptin, its role is opposite. Therefore, the gastric fundus is not the correct answer.

Hypothalamus
While the hypothalamus plays a central role in regulating appetite, it is not the site of leptin secretion. Rather, it serves as the target of leptin, where it modulates neuropeptides involved in hunger and satiety. In the clinical scenario, the hormone in question is being secreted, not received or processed, and thus, the hypothalamus is not the correct answer. Confusion may arise because ghrelin and leptin both act on the hypothalamus, but their sites of secretion are distinct. The hypothalamus, therefore, is not the source of the appetite-suppressing hormone.

Pancreatic islets
The pancreatic islets secrete hormones such as insulin, glucagon, and somatostatin, all of which influence metabolism but are not directly responsible for appetite suppression in this scenario. Although insulin has a complex interaction with satiety, it is not the hormone being targeted by the described drug trial. The stem focuses on leptin and ghrelin, neither of which originates from the pancreas. Therefore, despite its metabolic importance, the pancreatic islets are not the correct source of the hormone described. This makes the option incorrect in this clinical context.

stem: A 3-year-old boy has been brought into the GP surgery by his parents. He presents with pallor, lethargy and enlargement of the abdomen. The boy's parents said that they only noticed these symptoms for the past 2 weeks but it has been gradually worsening over the longer period. The boy was born in the UK by normal vaginal delivery following an uncomplicated pregnancy. There is no significant past medical history or recent travel history. The mother reports a family history of a form of metabolic disorder but couldn't remember the name. On examination, there is generalised pallor. There is enlargement of the abdomen with massive splenomegaly which is firm but not tender. Hepatomegaly is also noted. There is no jaundice or lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Gaucher's disease
Gaucher's disease is the most common lipid storage disorder and a cause of hepatosplenomegaly. Gaucher's disease is an autosomal recessive disease and it is the most common lipid storage disorder. It's a cause of hepatosplenomegaly. The family history in the history indicates Gaucher's disease as the most likely.

Heart failure
Heart failure is unusual in children and does not usually cause massive splenomegaly.

Chronic myeloid leukaemia
Chronic myeloid leukaemia can cause massive splenomegaly but it is unusual in children.

Acute myeloid leukaemia
Acute myeloid leukaemia can cause splenomegaly but massive splenomegaly is rare. It is not usually inherited.

Kala azar
Kala azar, also known as visceral leishmaniasis, is a cause of massive splenomegaly but given the lack of travel history, it is unlikely.

stem: A 2-year-old boy is admitted to the paediatric ward with his third episode of pneumococcal meningitis. His past medical history is significant for two episodes of severe pneumonia requiring hospitalisation. There is no family history of note and his immunisations are up-to-date. Physical examination is unremarkable apart from signs of meningism. A deficiency in which of the following proteins is the most likely underlying cause?
explanation:
C3
C3 deficiency - presents early in life with severe, recurrent bacterial infections, particularly encapsulated organisms. C3 is the central and most abundant component of the complement system, where all three pathways (classical, alternative, and lectin) converge. Cleavage of C3 into C3a and C3b is a critical step. C3b is a powerful opsonin, coating pathogens to facilitate their phagocytosis by cells like macrophages and neutrophils. This process is particularly vital for the clearance of encapsulated bacteria, such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Neisseria meningitidis, as their polysaccharide capsules resist phagocytosis. A deficiency in C3 leads to a profound failure of opsonisation, resulting in susceptibility to severe, recurrent, and lifethreatening pyogenic infections, typically presenting in early childhood, as seen in this 2-year-old boy with recurrent pneumococcal meningitis and pneumonia.

C1 inhibitor
C1 inhibitor deficiency is incorrect. A deficiency of C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) causes hereditary angioedema (HAE). C1-INH regulates the activity of the classical complement pathway and the contact system. Its absence leads to uncontrolled activation of these systems, resulting in the overproduction of bradykinin, a potent vasodilator that causes episodes of non-pitting, non-pruritic oedema of the skin, respiratory tract, and gastrointestinal tract. It is not associated with an increased susceptibility to pyogenic bacterial infections.

C1q
C1q deficiency is a less likely cause. C1q is a component of the C1 complex, which initiates the classical complement pathway. Deficiencies in early classical pathway components (C1, C2, C4) are most strongly associated with the development of autoimmune diseases, particularly Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE). This is thought to be due to impaired clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic cells. While there is an increased risk of infection with encapsulated organisms, it is generally less severe and less frequent than that seen in C3 deficiency.

C2
C2 deficiency is also incorrect. This is the most common inherited complement deficiency. Similar to C1q deficiency, it is primarily associated with an increased risk of autoimmune conditions like SLE. Patients can have an increased susceptibility to bacterial infections, particularly from encapsulated organisms, but the clinical phenotype is typically milder than that observed in C3 deficiency. The severe and recurrent nature of the infections in this young child makes C3 deficiency a much more probable diagnosis.

C5-9
C5-9 deficiency is incorrect. Deficiencies in the terminal complement components (C5, C6, C7, C8, or C9) impair the formation of the Membrane Attack Complex (MAC). The MAC is crucial for lysing certain pathogens, most notably Neisseria species. Therefore, individuals with C5-9 deficiencies have a significantly increased risk of recurrent and invasive infections with Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. They do not typically present with recurrent pneumococcal infections as seen in this case.

stem: Which one of the following syndromes is associated with an increased risk of Crohn's disease?
explanation:
Turner's syndrome
The correct answer is Turner's syndrome. Turner's syndrome, a genetic condition affecting only females, where one X chromosome is completely or partially absent, has been associated with an increased risk of developing Crohn's disease. The exact mechanism behind this association isn't fully understood but it is thought to be related to the altered immune function present in Turner's syndrome. In addition, women with Turner's syndrome often have malabsorption and other gastrointestinal issues that may predispose them to inflammatory bowel diseases like Crohn's.

Down's syndrome
Down's syndrome, also known as Trisomy 21, is not typically associated with an increased risk of Crohn's disease. Individuals with Down's syndrome are more likely to experience gastrointestinal problems such as Hirschsprung's disease, duodenal atresia, and coeliac disease but the incidence of inflammatory bowel disease like Crohn's does not appear to be elevated.

Fragile X syndrome
Fragile X syndrome is a genetic disorder leading to intellectual disability and behavioural challenges. While individuals with Fragile X can have various physical health issues including connective tissue problems and heart defects, there is no established link between Fragile X syndrome and an increased risk of developing Crohn's disease.

Patau syndrome
Patau Syndrome (Trisomy 13) is a severe genetic disorder associated with multiple congenital anomalies affecting many organ systems. However, this syndrome is not connected to an increased risk for Crohn's Disease. These patients' lifespan is usually significantly reduced due to their underlying conditions which makes it less likely for them to develop chronic diseases like Crohn's.

Edward's syndrome
Edward's Syndrome (Trisomy 18) is a severe genetic disorder associated with multiple congenital anomalies affecting many organ systems. However, this syndrome is not connected to an increased risk for Crohn's Disease. These patients' lifespan is usually significantly reduced due to their underlying conditions which makes it less likely for them to develop chronic diseases like Crohn's.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents with episodic burning pain in his hands and feet that worsens with physical activity or heat exposure. He also reports gastrointestinal discomfort and dark, reddish discolouration of the urine after exercise. Examination reveals clusters of small, dark red lesions on the lower abdomen and buttocks. His family history includes multiple relatives with kidney failure in their 40s and 50s. What is the most likely underlying mechanism of his condition?
explanation:
Deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A
Fabry disease is caused by a deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A. Deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A is the correct answer because the patient’s presentation is classic for Fabry disease, an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by a deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A. The resulting accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) in vascular endothelial cells and other tissues explains the burning pain in the hands and feet (acroparesthesias), dark red angiokeratomas on the lower abdomen, and dark-coloured urine indicative of renal involvement (hematuria or proteinuria). The family history of early-onset renal failure further supports this diagnosis, as Fabry disease often leads to progressive kidney damage and end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Worsening pain with heat or exercise is a characteristic feature of Fabry disease due to impaired small-fibre nerve function.

Defective collagen synthesis
Defective collagen synthesis is incorrect because it refers to conditions such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or Alport syndrome. Alport syndrome can lead to renal failure but is primarily associated with progressive hematuria, sensorineural hearing loss, and ocular abnormalities, none of which are described in this patient. Additionally, the presence of angiokeratomas and burning pain is not characteristic of collagen synthesis disorders, ruling out this option.

Immune-mediated vasculitis
Immune-mediated vasculitis, such as Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP) or ANCA-associated vasculitis, can cause renal involvement and purpuric skin lesions. However, vasculitis typically presents with systemic symptoms such as fever, malaise, and palpable purpura, which are not seen here. The dark red skin lesions in this patient are consistent with angiokeratomas rather than vasculitic purpura. Furthermore, the family history and specific neuropathic pain (acroparesthesias) are not characteristic of immune-mediated vasculitis.

Podocyte protein mutation
Podocyte protein mutations are associated with hereditary nephrotic syndromes such as congenital nephrotic syndrome (e.g., NPHS1 mutation). While podocyte dysfunction can lead to renal failure, it does not explain this patient’s systemic symptoms such as neuropathic pain, angiokeratomas, or exacerbation of symptoms with heat or exercise. The absence of nephrotic-range proteinuria and oedema also makes podocyte protein mutation an unlikely mechanism in this case.

Hyperglycemia-induced vascular damage
Hyperglycemia-induced vascular damage is incorrect because it refers to diabetic microvascular complications, including diabetic nephropathy and neuropathy. This patient’s young age, lack of diabetes history, and family history of renal failure without mention of hyperglycemia make this option less plausible. Additionally, the specific findings of angiokeratomas and exercise-induced pain are not features of diabetic complications.

stem: Which one of the following is equivalent to the pre-test probability?
explanation:
The prevalence of a condition
The correct answer is that the pre-test probability is equivalent to the prevalence of a condition. The pre-test probability represents the probability of a patient having a condition before any diagnostic test is performed, and this is fundamentally the same as the prevalence of that condition in the relevant population. This relationship forms the basis of Bayesian analysis in clinical diagnosis.

Post test odds / (1 + post-test odds)
Post test odds / (1 + post-test odds) is actually the formula for converting post-test odds to post-test probability. This mathematical transformation is necessary because clinicians typically work with probabilities rather than odds, but Bayes' theorem calculations are performed using odds.

Pre-test odds x likelihood ratio
Pre-test odds x likelihood ratio is the formula for calculating post-test odds, not pre-test probability. This calculation is used to update the probability of disease after obtaining new diagnostic information through a test.

The incidence of a condition
The incidence of a condition is incorrect because incidence measures new cases of a condition in a population over a specific time period, whereas pre-test probability reflects the existing burden of disease at a point in time.

Post-test odds / likelihood ratio
Post-test odds / likelihood ratio would mathematically yield the pretest odds, not the pre-test probability. This is essentially working backwards through Bayes' theorem, but still doesn't give us the pre-test probability, which is equivalent to prevalence.

stem: Which one of the following best describes the Bohr effect?
options: Increase in pO2 means CO2 binds less well to Hb
Decreasing acidity (or pCO2) means oxygen binds less well to Hb
Decrease in pO2 means CO2 binds less well to Hb
Raised 2,3-DPG enhances oxygen delivery to the tissues
Increasing acidity (or pCO2) means oxygen binds less well to Hb
explanation:
Increasing acidity (or pCO2) means oxygen binds less well to Hb
The Bohr effect describes how increasing acidity (or pCO2) means oxygen binds less well to Hb, which is the correct answer. This physiological phenomenon is crucial for tissue oxygenation, as it facilitates oxygen release from haemoglobin in metabolically active tissues where pH is lower and pCO2 is higher. The effect is mediated through conformational changes in the haemoglobin molecule when exposed to increased H+ concentration or CO2, reducing its affinity for oxygen.

Increase in pO2 means CO2 binds less well to Hb
Increase in pO2 means CO2 binds less well to Hb describes the Haldane effect, which is essentially the reverse of the Bohr effect. The Haldane effect explains how oxygenation of haemoglobin in the lungs promotes the release of CO2, facilitating its elimination.

Decreasing acidity (or pCO2) means oxygen binds less well to Hb
Decreasing acidity (or pCO2) means oxygen binds less well to Hb is incorrect as it states the opposite of the Bohr effect. In fact, decreasing acidity increases haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, which occurs in the lungs where pH is higher and pCO2 is lower.

Decrease in pO2 means CO2 binds less well to Hb
Decrease in pO2 means CO2 binds less well to Hb is incorrect as it describes a relationship that doesn't exist. Lower pO2 actually promotes CO2 binding to haemoglobin, which is part of the Haldane effect.

Raised 2,3-DPG enhances oxygen delivery to the tissues
Raised 2,3-DPG enhances oxygen delivery to the tissues is a true statement but describes a different physiological mechanism. While 2,3DPG does enhance oxygen delivery by shifting the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve to the right, this is not the Bohr effect. This mechanism becomes particularly important in conditions like chronic hypoxia where 2,3-DPG levels increase to facilitate oxygen delivery.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with burning pain in his hands and feet. His past medical history is significant for subcapsular cataracts, which he had surgically repaired two years ago. Systems review reveals frothy urine, and his family history is significant for a maternal grandfather who died from a heart attack in his 40s. On examination, there are multiple angiokeratomas on the chest and back. There are no focal neurological deficits and crude touch is intact. Urinalysis shows protein +++ and is negative for leucocytes and blood. What enzyme is most likely deficient?
explanation:
Alpha-galactosidase A
Fabry disease is caused by a deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A. This young male patient's glove and stocking neuropathy, cataracts, angiokeratomas, and proteinuria are very suggestive of Fabry disease.
