The carers report she has had very little oral intake over the last few days, requiring a lot of encouragement to eat. On assessment, the patient smells strongly of urine and has evidence of shock. A urine dip is positive for nitrates and leukocytes and a blood glucose recording is low. Urosepsis causing hypoglycaemia is suspected. As well as IV fluids and antibiotics glucose is provided orally and via IV as per hospital protocol. What part of the nephron is the majority of this substance normally reabsorbed?
explanation:
Proximal convoluted tubules
The majority of glucose reabsorption in the nephron occurs within the proximal convoluted tubule. Glucose is usually almost fully reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubules (PCT) by secondary active, sodium-coupled transporters (SGLT2).

Ascending loop of Henle
The ascending loop of Henle is made up of a thick and thin selection. Sodium, potassium and chloride ions are all reabsorbed in this segment of the nephrons via active transport, but glucose reabsorption is low.

Collecting tubules
Collecting tubules are the final component of the kidney to influence substance and fluid reabsorption. This section of the nephrons is responsible for approximately 5% of sodium reabsorption and between 5% and 25% of water, depending on the level of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). Glucose reabsorption in the collecting tubules is very low.

Descending loop of Henle
The descending loop of Henle functions in connection with the ascending loop of Henle to control ion and water reabsorption. The descending aspect has low permeability to most ions resulting in a high level of water reabsorption. Again, glucose reabsorption is low.

Distal convoluted tubules
Distal convoluted tubules (DCT) plays a role in the regulation of potassium, sodium, calcium and pH. Several active and passive mechanisms are involved with the regulation of these ions which are affected by circulatory hormone levels (e.g. aldosterone). Almost all the glucose has already been reabsorbed by the time the filtrate reaches the DCT, reabsorption at this section is low.

stem: A new point-of-care test has been developed to detect individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19). Over 3 months, 1100 patients who attended the emergency department were randomly selected to be tested for COVID-19. The new point-of-care test was positive in 150 of these patients, of which 100 had COVID-19 infection confirmed by PCR. COVID-19 was also confirmed by PCR test in 30 of the patients who tested negative on the new point-of-care test. What is the positive predictive value (PPV) of the new point-of-care test?
explanation:
66.7%
Positive predictive value = TP / (TP + FP) The positive predictive value (PPV) is calculated using the true positives (TP) and false positives (FP). PPV = TP / (TP + FP). In this case, TP = the 100 patients who tested positive with the new test and were confirmed to have COVID-19 by PCR. FP = those who tested positive with the new test but did not have COVID-19 confirmed by PCR, which is 50 patients (150 total positive - 100 true positives). So, PPV = 100 / (100 + 50) = 0.6667 or 66.7%. Therefore, the correct answer is 66.7%.

76.9%
76.9% is incorrect. This is the sensitivity of the test. Sensitivity is calculated using the true positives (TP) and false negatives (FN). Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN). In this scenario, FN = the 30 patients who tested negative with the new test but were confirmed positive on PCR.

94.8%
94.8% is incorrect. This is the specificity of the test. Specificity is calculated using the true negatives (TN) and false positives (FP). Specificity = TN / (TN + FP). In this scenario, TN = the 920 patients who tested negative with the new test and were confirmed negative with PCR.

96.8%
96.8% is incorrect. This is the negative predictive value (NPV). NPV is calculated using the true negatives (TN) and false negatives (FN). NPV= TN / (TN + FN).

98.4%
98.4% is incorrect. As above, in this scenario PPV = 100 / (100 + 50) = 66.7%.

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents to the emergency department following a fall at home, sustaining a head injury. She has a past medical history of atrial fibrillation, and is taking warfarin for stroke prophylaxis, with a target INR of 2.5. CT head demonstrates an acute subdural haemorrhage. Her INR is 5.5. You decide to administer IV vitamin K 5mg. What is the mechanism of action of this medication?
options: Acts as a co-factor in the carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X
Acts as a co-factor in the carboxylation of factors II, V, X and XII
explanation:
Acts as a co-factor in the carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X
Vitamin K acts as a cofactor in the carboxylation of clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X). In this scenario, as the patient has presented with major bleeding on warfarin, IV vitamin K should be given to reverse the effects of warfarin, by allowing the carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X.

Activates anti-thrombin III
Vitamin K does not activate anti-thrombin III. Heparin works by activating anti-thrombin III, which inactivates factor Xa and thrombin.

Direct inhibitor of factor Xa
The DOACs apixaban, edoxaban and rivaroxaban work by directly inhibiting factor Xa. Vitamin K does not directly inhibit factor Xa.

Direct thrombin inhibitor
Dabigatran (also a DOAC) works by directly inhibiting thrombin (factor IIa). Vitamin K does not directly inhibit thrombin.

stem: A 55-year-old male with a history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension is participating in a randomized controlled trial (RCT) comparing two antihypertensive drugs. After three months, he decides to withdraw from the study due to personal reasons. The trial's primary outcome is the reduction in systolic blood pressure at six months. When analysing the results, how should this patient be included?
options: Exclude him from the analysis since he withdrew early
Include him only if he completed at least half of the study duration
Analyse his data separately as part of a per-protocol analysis
Use his baseline data for endpoint estimation
explanation:
Include him in the analysis
In an intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis, all participants originally allocated to each treatment arm are included in the final analysis, regardless of whether they completed or adhered to the protocol. This approach maintains randomization benefits and provides an unbiased estimate of treatment effect by reflecting real-world scenarios where not all patients adhere to treatment.

Exclude him from the analysis since he withdrew early
Excluding participants who withdraw can introduce bias and compromise randomization integrity, potentially skewing results towards those more compliant with treatment or those who had less severe disease. ITT avoids these biases by including all initially randomized patients.

Include him only if he completed at least half of the study duration
This method would also introduce bias, as it selectively includes participants based on adherence or other factors that may correlate with outcomes, thus distorting true treatment effects.

Analyse his data separately as part of a per-protocol analysis
A per-protocol analysis includes only those participants who completed the study according to its protocol. While it can provide insights into efficacy under ideal conditions, it lacks generalizability and does not reflect typical clinical practice where non-adherence occurs.

Use his baseline data for endpoint estimation
Using baseline data alone does not account for changes over time or interventions' potential effects; hence it fails to capture true outcomes influenced by treatments within trials.

stem: A 65-year-old woman attends the clinic with a 6-month history of progressive shortness of breath on exertion. She has a past medical history of severe COPD for which she is on long-term oxygen therapy for. On examination, you note pitting oedema to the mid thighs, raised JVP with a prominent V wave, a precordial heave, and a loud P2. Based on the likely diagnosis, what mechanism is most likely implicated?
options: Pulmonary arteries vasoconstriction due to hypercapnia
Pulmonary arteries vasoconstriction due to hypoxia
Pulmonary arteries vasodilation due to hypoxia
Pulmonary veins vasoconstriction due to hypoxia
Pulmonary veins vasodilation due to hypoxia
explanation:
Pulmonary arteries vasoconstriction due to hypoxia
Pulmonary arteries vasoconstrict in the presence of hypoxia. This patient's presentation is consistent with cor pulmonale secondary to COPD. The hypoxic vasoconstriction of pulmonary arteries is a key pathophysiological mechanism in the development of pulmonary hypertension and subsequent right heart failure in COPD patients. This reflex, known as the Euler-Liljestrand mechanism, causes vasoconstriction of small pulmonary arteries in response to alveolar hypoxia, initially serving as an adaptive response to redirect blood flow to better-ventilated areas of the lung. However, in chronic hypoxic states like COPD, this leads to sustained pulmonary hypertension.

Pulmonary arteries vasoconstriction due to hypercapnia
Pulmonary arteries vasoconstriction due to hypercapnia is incorrect. While hypercapnia can cause some vasoconstriction of pulmonary vessels, it is not the primary mechanism in COPD-related pulmonary hypertension. The hypoxic response is much more significant in driving the pathological changes.

Pulmonary arteries vasodilation due to hypoxia
Pulmonary arteries vasodilation due to hypoxia is incorrect. Hypoxia causes vasoconstriction, not vasodilation, in the pulmonary circulation. This is opposite to the systemic circulation where hypoxia typically causes vasodilation.

Pulmonary veins vasoconstriction due to hypoxia
Pulmonary veins vasoconstriction due to hypoxia is incorrect. The pulmonary veins play a minimal role in pulmonary hypertension in COPD. The primary changes occur in the pulmonary arterial circulation, not the venous system.

Pulmonary veins vasodilation due to hypoxia
Pulmonary veins vasodilation due to hypoxia is incorrect. Pulmonary veins are not significantly affected by hypoxia in terms of their tone, and vasodilation of pulmonary veins is not a feature of cor pulmonale or COPD-related pulmonary hypertension.

stem: Which one of the following statements regarding vitamin D-resistant rickets is false?
options: Management includes the use of high-dose vitamin D supplements
Failure to thrive may be seen
explanation:
Decreased urinary phosphate is characteristic
The correct answer is decreased urinary phosphate. Vitamin D-resistant rickets, also known as X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets, is characterised by increased urinary phosphate excretion due to defective proximal tubular reabsorption of phosphate. This leads to hypophosphataemia, which is a hallmark of the condition. The increased urinary phosphate excretion occurs despite normal or low serum calcium and normal or elevated PTH levels.

Management includes the use of high-dose vitamin D supplements
Management includes the use of high-dose vitamin D supplements is correct. Treatment typically involves high doses of activated vitamin D (calcitriol) along with oral phosphate supplements. This combination therapy aims to normalise serum phosphate levels and improve bone mineralisation.

Is a X-linked dominant condition
Is a X-linked dominant condition is correct. The condition is caused by mutations in the PHEX gene located on the X chromosome. It follows X-linked dominant inheritance, meaning both males and females can be affected, and an affected parent has a 50% chance of passing the condition to their children.

X-ray changes include cupped metaphyses
X-ray changes include cupped metaphyses is correct. Radiological findings are similar to those seen in nutritional rickets, including cupping and fraying of the metaphyses, widening of the growth plates, and bowing of the long bones. These changes result from impaired mineralisation of newly formed bone.

Failure to thrive may be seen
Failure to thrive may be seen is correct. Children with vitamin D-resistant rickets often present with growth failure, short stature, and skeletal deformities. The impaired bone mineralisation and metabolic derangements can affect overall growth and development.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is reviewed in the endocrine clinic with a history of short stature, primary amenorrhoea, and mild hearing loss. She is on oestrogen replacement therapy and has no significant past medical history. Examination reveals a high-arched palate, low hairline, and a broad chest with widely spaced nipples. Her BMI is 22 kg/m². She is otherwise well and lives independently. What is the most serious long-term health risk in this patient?
explanation:
Aortic dilatation
An increased risk of aortic dilatation and dissection are the most serious long-term health problems for women with Turner's syndrome. Aortic dilatation is correct because the patient has clinical features consistent with Turner’s syndrome, including short stature, primary amenorrhoea, and characteristic physical findings such as a high-arched palate, low hairline, and widely spaced nipples. Turner’s syndrome is associated with a range of cardiovascular anomalies, the most serious of which is progressive aortic dilatation, which can lead to dissection or rupture. This risk is increased even in the absence of hypertension or aortic valve abnormalities, and cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of mortality in affected individuals. Lifelong cardiac monitoring is essential.

Aortic stenosis
Aortic stenosis is incorrect because although it can occur in patients with Turner syndrome due to bicuspid aortic valve, it is not the most serious long-term risk. The more significant concern is progressive aortic root dilatation, which can lead to dissection or rupture—major causes of premature mortality in this population. Aortic stenosis typically presents later and progresses gradually, and while it may require monitoring, it is less immediately life-threatening than aortic dissection.

Coronary artery disease
Coronary artery disease is incorrect because although individuals with Turner’s syndrome may develop features of metabolic syndrome, including dyslipidaemia and hypertension, the risk of coronary events tends to occur later in life. With appropriate management, including aspirin and statins when indicated, the condition is generally modifiable and not the most immediate life-threatening concern.

Ischaemic stroke
Ischaemic stroke is incorrect because although Turner syndrome may be associated with vascular risk factors such as hypertension or congenital cardiovascular anomalies, ischaemic stroke is not considered a typical or leading complication. The most serious long-term risk is aortic dilatation, which can lead to dissection and sudden death. This risk often develops silently and requires active surveillance. While stroke is a serious condition, it is not as strongly linked to Turner syndrome nor as life-threatening in this context as aortic dissection.

Left ventricular aneurysm
Left ventricular aneurysm is incorrect because it is a rare complication that usually arises after myocardial infarction, which is not a recognised feature of Turner syndrome. There is no indication of ischaemic heart disease in this young woman, and her history and presentation do not support a prior cardiac event. While serious, this diagnosis would not be relevant in the absence of prior infarction or significant structural heart disease.

stem: A 7-year-old child presents to the GP with generalised burning pain and paraesthesia across the body. On examination, a number of angiokeratomas are noted, and whilst examining other symptoms, the GP notes that the lenses are opacified. Urinalysis reveals proteinuria. The GP refers the patient onto the local paediatrics team. Ultimately, a diagnosis of Fabry disease is made. How is this disease inherited?
explanation:
X-linked recessive
Fabry disease is a rare condition, part of the group of conditions known as lysosomal storage disorders. It is characterised by the signs and symptoms described in this scenario, along with early cardiovascular disease. It is caused by a deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A and is inherited in an X-linked recessive fashion.

Autosomal dominant
The other answers are thus incorrect.

Autosomal recessive
The other answers are thus incorrect.

Mitochondrial inheritance
The other answers are thus incorrect.

X-linked dominant
The other answers are thus incorrect.

stem: Which part of an antibody do immune cells bind to?
explanation:
Fc region
Immune cells bind to the crystallising region (Fc) of immunoglobulins. The Fc region is the tail region of an antibody that interacts with cell surface receptors.

stem: A 32-year-old mum attends the GP surgery with her newborn son for the six-week check. During which, she brought up that her son developed vitamin K deficiency bleeding when he was three-days-old. He has made a good recovery since and is on vitamin K replacement. Which of the following clotting factor is dependent on this vitamin?
explanation:
Clotting factor II
The correct answer is clotting factor II. The formation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X, as well as protein C, S and Z, are dependent on vitamin K.

Clotting factor I
Vitamin K acts as a cofactor in the carboxylation of clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X). Clotting factor I (fibrinogen) is not dependent on vitamin K.

Clotting factor V
Vitamin K acts as a cofactor in the carboxylation of clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X). Clotting factor V is not dependent on vitamin K.

Clotting factor VIII
Vitamin K acts as a cofactor in the carboxylation of clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X). Clotting factor VIII is not dependent on vitamin K.

Clotting factor XII
Vitamin K acts as a cofactor in the carboxylation of clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X). Clotting factor XII is not dependent on vitamin K.

stem: A 36-year-old Turkish male attends the rheumatology clinic with painful orogenital ulceration, uveitis, and non-erosive polyarthritis. He has a positive pathergy test. Which human leukocyte antigen (HLA) subtype and chromosome is associated with the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
HLA-B51 on chromosome 6
HLA antigens are encoded for by genes on chromosome 6. HLA-B51 on chromosome 6 is the correct answer. The presence of painful orogenital ulceration, uveitis, and non-erosive polyarthritis is highly suggestive of Behçet's disease. It occurs most commonly in people from the Middle East and Asia. The pathergy test has a 95-99% specificity for Behçet's disease. Behçet's disease is strongly associated with HLA-B51 on chromosome 6.

HLA-DR3 on chromosome 8
HLA-DR3 on chromosome 8 is an incorrect answer. The HLA gene complex is located on a 3 megabase pair (Mbp) length within chromosome 6p21. HLA-DR3 is associated with type 1 diabetes mellitus and rheumatoid arthritis.

HLA-B27 on chromosome 6
HLA-B27 on chromosome 6 is an incorrect answer. HLA-B27 is commonly associated with ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis (formerly known as Reiter's syndrome), and acute anterior uveitis. However, HLA-B27 can also occur in Behçet's disease in addition to HLA-B51. It appears that symptoms tend to be milder when both HLA-B27 and HLA-B51 are present.

HLA-B27 on chromosome 8
HLA-B27 on chromosome 8 is an incorrect answer. The HLA gene complex is located on a 3 Mbp length within chromosome 6p21.

HLA-B51 on chromosome 8
HLA-B51 on chromosome 8 is an incorrect answer. The HLA gene complex is located on a 3 Mbp length within chromosome 6p21.

stem: A 58-year-old woman is seen in a respiratory clinic. She has progressive breathlessness and recent pulmonary vascular testing has confirmed pulmonary hypertension. Due to the deterioration of symptoms, it is decided to start her on bosentan. What is the best description of its action?
explanation:
Endothelin antagonist
Bosentan is a non-selective endothelin antagonist. Endothelin causes pulmonary vasoconstriction and therefore antagonists can be used to treat pulmonary hypertension. It can be associated with abnormalities in liver function tests (LFTs) and so regular LFTs are needed during treatment.

Endothelin agonist
Endothelin agonists would enhance the action of endothelin and hence cause increased pulmonary vasoconstriction, this would not be suitable to treat pulmonary hypertension.

Guanylate cyclase stimulator
Guanylate cyclase stimulators such as riociguat works in synergy with nitric oxide to have vasodilatory properties which can be used to treat pulmonary hypertension.

Phosphodiesterase inhibitor
Sildenafil is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor that works to treat pulmonary hypertension by selectively reducing pulmonary vascular tone.

Prostaglandin agonist
Prostaglandin agonists cause vasodilation, prevent platelet aggregation and inhibit vascular proliferation and can be used to treat pulmonary hypertension.

stem: A 21-year-old, with type 1 diabetes and depression is brought in having been found confused and 'acting drunk' before collapsing at home. Her parents confirm she has been very low in mood recently and has talked about taking her own life. They are concerned as on finding her they noticed her injectable medication also out on the floor. On exam, she is sweaty and only responsive to pain. Her observations are: Heart rate 108/min BP 122/80 mmHg Oxygen saturations 98% Temperature 36.7 ºC Blood glucose 1.9mmol/L What receptor type is bound to by the medication this patient has most likely overdosed on?
explanation:
Tyrosine kinase
Insulin binds to a receptor tyrosine kinase in the cell membrane. This patient has presented following an insulin overdose. The main features of insulin overdose are a result of hypoglycaemia (noted on this patient's observation) and include sweating, confusion, and drowsiness/reduced consciousness. Insulin binds to tyrosine kinase, a type of enzyme receptor in the cell membrane, resulting in a signal transduction cascade, activating enzymes and transcription factors within the cell that mediates the intracellular effects of insulin. Other tyrosine kinase receptors include insulin-like growth factor (IGF) and epidermal growth factor (EGF).

G protein-coupled
G protein-coupled receptors are activated by a wide range of extracellular signals/ligands such as peptide hormones, lipophilic hormones, and biogenic amines (e.g., adrenaline) however insulin does not bind to these receptors. G protein-coupled receptors can stimulate adenylate cyclase, inhibit adenylate cyclase, or activate phospholipase C and in general mediate slow transmission and affect metabolic processes.

Guanylate cyclase
Guanylate cyclase receptors are transmembrane proteins that span the lipid bilayer only once. They contain intrinsic enzyme activity and include atrial natriuretic factor and brain natriuretic peptide. Again, insulin does not bind or affect these receptors.

Ligand-gated ion channel
Ligand-gated ion channel receptors are transmembrane proteins which open to allow ions (e.g., Na+, K+, Ca2+) to pass through in response to the binding of chemical messengers/ligand. This ion movement results in processes such as depolarisation or hyperpolarisation within cells. A number of ligands can open these channels but insulin is not one of them.

Serine/threonine kinase
Serine/threonine kinase is another form of enzyme receptor similar to tyrosine kinase but is not affected/bound by insulin. These receptors instead are bound by the ligand transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) which plays an important role in wound healing, immunoregulation, and cancer.

stem: A new blood test which can show signs of myocardial damage within one hour of the onset of chest pain is developed. In a trial of 100 patients presenting with chest pain, 40 of the patients are later proven to have had myocardial ischaemia by conventional troponin tests. Of these patients the new test was positive in 20 cases. The new test was also positive in 20 of the remaining 60 patients later shown to have a negative troponin. What is the negative predictive value of the new test for myocardial ischaemia?
explanation:
0.66
Negative predictive value = TN / (TN + FN) The new test was negative in 20 of the patients later shown to have myocardial ischaemia (false negative) and negative in 40 patients confirmed not to have myocardial ischaemia (true negative) Negative predictive value = TN / (TN + FN) = 40 / (40 + 20) = 0.66

Cannot calculate
Cannot calculate is incorrect because the negative predictive value can be calculated using the given data.

stem: A 26-year-old man is reviewed in the Medical Admissions Unit due to a hot, swollen left leg, which he had first noticed the day before. He was born in Kazakhstan and migrated to the UK two years ago. He is very short-sighted, and was diagnosed with learning difficulties at school, but denies any other medical problems. On inspection, he is tall and slim, with long fingers and a kyphotic spine. His cheeks appear flushed, though he is not peripherally vasodilated elsewhere. Examination of his abdomen, as well as cardiovascular, respiratory and neurological systems, are all normal. His calf measurements and D-dimer blood test result are shown below: Left calf 35cm Right calf 41cm D-dimer 3500ug/L (<500) What is the most likely underlying pathology?
explanation:
Homocystinuria
The unifying diagnosis in this patient is homocystinuria - an autosomal recessive condition caused by defects in methionine metabolism. Features consistent with homocystinuria in this patient include malar flush, tall stature, arachnodactyly, myopia, learning difficulties and unprovoked DVT at a young age. The significance of his immigration status is that babies born in the UK would usually be screened for homocystinuria via the newborn heel prick test, whereas this may have been missed in the given scenario.

Cystinuria
Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive condition caused by inadequate reabsorption of cysteine in the proximal convoluted tubule, leading to recurrent nephrocalcinosis. This does not explain the patient's myopia, learning difficulties, or arachnodactyly.

Behçet's disease
Behçet's disease is a reasonable diagnosis to consider when dealing with a patient from Central Asia with an unprovoked DVT at a young age - however, nearly all patients with Behçet's disease present with ulcerations, usually of the mouth. Other 'hallmark' symptoms of Behçet's include uveitis or iritis; genital ulcers and skin lesions such as folliculitis, which are not seen here. Behçet's does not provide an explanation for this patient's myopia, learning difficulties, or arachnodactyly.

Phenylketonuria
Phenylketonuria is a different inborn error of metabolism that can lead to learning difficulties and is usually picked up on the heel prick test. However, the other common defining feature of phenylketonuria is seizure activity, rather than any of the signs and symptoms described in this patient.

Tay-Sachs disease
Tay-Sachs disease is a rare lysosomal storage disorder, which is associated with progressive neurological deterioration and is usually fatal before adulthood. This does not explain the patient's myopia, learning difficulties, or arachnodactyly.

stem: Which one of the following statements regarding interleukin 1 (IL-1) is true?
options: It is released mainly by macrophages/monocytes
It reduces expression of selectin molecules on the endothelium
IL-1 antagonists are currently licensed for use in colorectal cancer
It inhibits the release of nitric oxide by the endothelium
explanation:
It is released mainly by macrophages/monocytes
Interleukin-1 (IL-1) is a pro-inflammatory cytokine that plays a central role in the regulation of immune and inflammatory responses. It is primarily produced and released by activated macrophages and monocytes, although other cell types such as endothelial cells, epithelial cells, and fibroblasts can also produce IL-1 under certain conditions.

It causes vasoconstriction
The statement It causes vasoconstriction is incorrect. In fact, IL-1 has been shown to cause vasodilation rather than vasoconstriction. This vasodilatory effect contributes to the increased blood flow and redness seen in areas of inflammation.

It reduces expression of selectin molecules on the endothelium
The statement It reduces expression of selectin molecules on the endothelium is also incorrect. On the contrary, IL-1 increases the expression of selectin molecules on the endothelium. Selectins are adhesion molecules that facilitate leukocyte rolling along the vascular wall, an early step in leukocyte extravasation during inflammation.

IL-1 antagonists are currently licensed for use in colorectal cancer
Regarding IL-1 antagonists are currently licensed for use in colorectal cancer, this too is not accurate. While IL-1 antagonists, such as anakinra, have been investigated for their potential anti-cancer effects due to their ability to modulate inflammation, they are not currently licensed for use in colorectal cancer in the UK.

It inhibits the release of nitric oxide by the endothelium
The claim that It inhibits the release of nitric oxide by the endothelium is false. Rather than inhibiting its release, IL-1 actually stimulates nitric oxide production by inducing nitric oxide synthase activity. Nitric oxide plays several roles in inflammation including vasodilation and modulation of leukocyte behaviour.

stem: The general surgery department is trying to establish a best practice prophylactic antibiotic policy with regard to surgical site infections. To do so, they design a study, which examines whether a group of similarly matched patients (Group A) given antibiotic A develop a higher rate of post-operative surgical site infections when compared to a group (Group B) given antibiotic B. The proportion of patients in groups A and B developing surgical site infections are recorded. What is the best test to determine if there is a statistically significant difference between the two groups?
explanation:
Chi-squared test
Chi-squared test is the correct answer. This study seeks to determine the percentage of wound infections developing in groups A and B and determine whether there is a difference. The Chi-squared test is a statistical test used to compare percentages i.e. the proportion of patients that improved/worsened after a specific intervention. This is non-parametric data.

Mann-Whitney U test
Mann-Whitney U test is incorrect. This statistical test is used to measure ordinal, interval or ratio scales of unpaired data. An example of an ordinal variable is Likert items e.g. a 5 point scale. This is not the correct test to compare percentages.

Student's t-test (paired)
Student's t-test (paired) is incorrect. The student's t-test must be used with data that are normally distributed. This is not the case in this question. Additionally, a paired student's t-test involves two sets of observations from the same sample e.g. before and after measurements for the same group of people.

Student's t-test (unpaired)
Student's t-test (unpaired) is incorrect. The data is not normally distributed and therefore a non-parametric test is appropriate.

Wilcoxon sign rank test
Wilcoxon signed-rank test is incorrect. This is the non-parametric equivalent of the paired t-test. It measures before and after results from the same test population. Therefore it is not indicated in this case.

stem: An 18-year-old woman presents to the endocrine clinic after being referred by her GP due to primary amenorrhoea. Her history indicates that she was born at term without complications and had normal prenatal testing. On physical examination, she is noted to be short in stature with low-set ears and a webbed neck. No cardiac murmurs are detected on auscultation. Laboratory results are as follows: Free T3 4.2 (3.5-7.8 pmol/L) Free T4 14.7 (9.0-25.0 pmol/L) TSH 2.1 (0.4-4.0 mU/L) What is the most serious long-term complication associated with her underlying condition?
explanation:
Aortic dilatation
An increased risk of aortic dilatation and dissection are the most serious long-term health problems for women with Turner's syndrome. Aortic dilatation is the most serious long-term complication of Turner syndrome, with an increased risk of progression to aortic dissection or aneurysm. Consequently, adults with this condition undergo regular surveillance to allow early detection and treatment. Additional cardiac complications commonly associated with Turner syndrome include bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta.

Atrial septal defect
Atrial septal defects (ASD) and other septal defects are not typically seen in Turner syndrome. ASD is more frequently encountered in Down syndrome, with as many as half being affected by a septal defect as well as being at risk of other valvular and structural abnormalities.

Mitral valve prolapse
Mitral valve prolapse, while not strongly connected to Turner syndrome, can present with a range of symptoms, from light-headedness and palpitations to syncope or even sudden death. It should be considered in patients displaying marfanoid habitus who present with syncope or have a family history of premature sudden cardiac death, as it may be inherited, particularly in Marfan syndrome.

Pulmonary valve stenosis
Pulmonary valve stenosis has no significant association with Turner syndrome but should be considered in individuals exhibiting features such as short stature, ptosis, and hypertelorism suggestive of Noonan syndrome, along with symptoms like fatigue and breathlessness. Additionally, the absence of a murmur does not rule out valvular disease but its presence would increase suspicion; however, it seems unlikely in this case due to the lack of reported symptoms.

Ventricular septal defect
A ventricular septal defect is unlikely here as she is asymptomatic and this commonly presents in infancy with failure to thrive if the defect is small or symptoms of heart failure if larger. A small VSD can persist to adulthood, leading to the development of Eisenmenger syndrome due to the reversal of the left-right shunt. VSDs are also not typically associated with Turner syndrome but can be seen more frequently in Down syndrome and DiGeorge syndrome.

stem: A 22-year-old man has had 3 months of painless, progressive vision loss. This was first in the right eye and is now affecting the left. His mother, two maternal uncles, and maternal grandmother are also affected. Visual acuity is reduced significantly in both eyes, along with bilateral central scotomas and severe dyschromatopsia. His pupils are equal and reactive. Fundoscopy reveals hyperaemic optic discs with subtle peripapillary telangiectasia, and no disc oedema. What is the inheritance pattern of the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Mitochondrial
Leber's Hereditary Optic Neuropathy: mitochondrial inheritance pattern. This patient most likely has Leber's Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON), which is caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA affecting the respiratory chain, and demonstrates a mitochondrial inheritance pattern. This presents in young adults (20-30 years old) with central scotoma, dyschromatopsia, and rapid visual loss, as seen in this patient. Fundoscopy showing hyperaemic optic discs with peripapillary telangiectasia without disc oedema supports this diagnosis. Besides the patient, only maternal relatives (mother, maternal uncles, and maternal grandmother) are affected, with no evidence of male-to-offspring transmission, consistent with mitochondrial DNA being inherited exclusively from the mother. Since mitochondria are transmitted via oocytes and sperm contributes no mitochondria to a zygote at fertilisation, a mother will pass LHON to all of her children. Affected males do not transmit the disease to offspring. While all children of affected females inherit the mitochondrial mutation, not all will develop the condition, as LHON shows incomplete penetrance, particularly in females. Environmental and genetic factors likely influence whether the disease manifests.

Autosomal dominant
Autosomal dominant is incorrect as LHON demonstrates mitochondrial inheritance and the family history shows no male-to-offspring transmission. In autosomal dominant disorders, both males and females can transmit the disease, which is not mentioned here. This option could be considered if both maternal and paternal sides showed transmission from affected males and females. An example of this is autosomal dominant optic atrophy (DOA), linked to OPA1 mutations, which typically presents with gradual bilateral vision loss in childhood, disc pallor rather than hyperaemia, and no maternal-only inheritance.

Autosomal recessive
Autosomal recessive is incorrect as LHON demonstrates mitochondrial inheritance, and all generations are affected in this scenario, making autosomal recessive inheritance unlikely. This could be considered in Wolfram syndrome, which is autosomal recessive. Alongside optic atrophy, it presents with associated with diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, and deafness, which are not seen here.

X-linked dominant
X-linked dominant is incorrect as LHON demonstrates mitochondrial inheritance and the family history only shows individuals affected on the mother's side, with no clear pattern of male-to-female transmission. In X-linked dominant disorders, affected males transmit the condition to all their daughters but none of their sons, and affected females can transmit to both sexes, resulting in a characteristic pedigree with sex-specific transmission patterns. An example X-linked dominant disorder that can cause retinal abnormalities is incontinentia pigmenti. However, this primarily affects females and is usually lethal in males, and is associated with skin abnormalities (e.g. blistering and hyperpigmentation in infancy), dental anomalies, alopecia, and central nervous system involvement (e.g. seizures and developmental delay). Fundoscopy would also show retinal ischaemia, neovascularisation, and optic nerve atrophy instead.

X-linked recessive
X-linked recessive is incorrect as LHON demonstrates mitochondrial inheritance and both sexes are affected in this patient's family history. X-linked recessive disorders predominantly affect males, and transmission via unaffected carrier females would be expected. In this case, the mother is also affected. An example is choroideremia, which presents with night blindness and peripheral vision loss, not central vision loss with scotomas. Fundoscopy in X-linked recessive conditions like choroideremia shows widespread chorioretinal degeneration, unlike the hyperaemic discs and peripapillary telangiectasia seen here.

stem: What is the main advantage of non-inferiority trials when testing a new drug?
options: Useful for conditions where there is no proven drug treatment
Useful for conditions where there is a high placebo response rate
explanation:
Small sample size is required
The correct answer is small sample size is required. Non-inferiority trials are designed to demonstrate that a new treatment is not unacceptably worse than an existing treatment by a pre-specified margin. These trials typically require smaller sample sizes compared to superiority trials because they only need to show the new treatment is not significantly worse, rather than proving it is better. This makes them more efficient and cost-effective to conduct.

Prevents ethical dilemmas
Prevents ethical dilemmas is incorrect. Non-inferiority trials can actually create ethical challenges, particularly around determining what constitutes an acceptable margin of inferiority and whether it is ethical to potentially expose patients to a slightly less effective treatment.

Robust results are produced
Robust results are produced is incorrect. Non-inferiority trials are actually considered less robust than superiority trials because they are more susceptible to bias and their conclusions can be more difficult to interpret. Poor trial conduct tends to bias results towards non-inferiority.

Useful for conditions where there is no proven drug treatment
Useful for conditions where there is no proven drug treatment is incorrect. Non-inferiority trials require an established effective treatment to compare against. They cannot be used when there is no proven treatment - in these situations, superiority trials against placebo would be more appropriate.

Useful for conditions where there is a high placebo response rate
Useful for conditions where there is a high placebo response rate is incorrect. A high placebo response rate actually makes it more difficult to demonstrate non-inferiority as it reduces the apparent treatment effect of both the new and established drug. This would require larger sample sizes to maintain statistical power.

stem: A researcher is conducting a meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials into the use of an existing drug for the treatment of COVID-19. The studies compare the use of the drug and standard care against a placebo and standard care. He has plotted the studies on an axis with the treatment effect (odds ratio of in-hospital mortality due to COVID-19) on the horizontal axis and the standard error of the effect estimate on the vertical axis. Which type of plot has been drawn?
explanation:
Funnel plot
Funnel plots - show publication bias in meta-analyses A funnel plot is a meta-analytic plot with effect size (e.g. odds ratio) on the horizontal axis and a measure of the studies' standard error on the vertical axis (which is linked to study size). A symmetrical funnel plot suggests a lack of publication bias. An asymmetric funnel plot may be due to effects including publication bias or study heterogeneity. This BMJ paper describes how to interpret a funnel plot. Sterne J et al. Recommendations for examining and interpreting funnel plot asymmetry in meta-analyses of randomised controlled trials BMJ 2011; 343 :d4002.

Box plot
A box plot is used to plot the median and quartiles of a data set. They are useful as they are non-parametric and make no assumptions about the underlying statistical distribution of the data.

Forest plot
A forest plot is the main meta-analytic plot used to display the results of multiple studies, usually stacked vertically with the odds ratio on the horizontal axis.

Histogram
A histogram is used to represent the distribution of numerical data. Data are organised into bins containing a range of values. If the bins are equal size, the height of the chart on the vertical axis represents the frequency of observation.

Normal Q-Q plot
A normal Q-Q plot is a type of scatter plot which graphs theoretical quantiles against observed quantiles. It can help assess if a data-set came from a theoretical distribution e.g. the Normal distribution, which is important to decide if we can use parametric statistical methods like the t-test.

stem: A 3-year-old child is yet to learn to walk and the parents say used to be very floppy. The parents also state that their child is having more seizures recently and is bumping into objects crawling around the home regularly. The general examination is unremarkable, with no organomegaly detected, but there is apparent muscle stiffness of the limbs. Upon fundoscopy there are red areas seen on the macular. What is the clinical diagnosis?
explanation:
Tay-Sachs disease
Tay-Sachs disease typically presents with developmental delay and cherry red spot on the macula, without hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. This can present after 3 months of age as hypotonia, muscle weakness and myoclonic jerks and then progress to psychomotor retardation and regression, muscle spasticity, recurrent seizures, dementia and eventual death in early childhood. The cherry red spot in the macular is present in 90%. This is the classic infantile form described here, but there are also rarer juvenile and adultonset forms of the lysosomal storage disease.

Fabry disease
Fabry disease is incorrect. Although this is another lysosomal storage disease it presents differently to Tay-Sachs, being generally later onset and acroparesthesia, angiokeratomas and GI disturbance being the most common initial symptoms. This is followed by corneal blurring and eventual renal and/or cardiac failure in later life.

Gaucher's disease
Gaucher's disease is incorrect, as this disease presents with hepatosplenomegaly as glucocerebrosidase accumulates in the liver and spleen. However, it does cause developmental delay through accumulation in the brain. It is the most common form of lysosomal storage disease.

Krabbe's disease
Krabbe's disease is incorrect, as even though this lipid storage disease presents similarly to Tay-Sachs with developmental delays/regression and seizures, it also generally has an earlier onset and poorer prognosis, and with progressive demyelination leading to death by respiratory arrest or the complications thereof.

Niemann-Pick disease
Niemann-Pick disease is incorrect. Tay-Sachs and Niemann-Pick present very similarly, however the latter would include hepatosplenomegaly on the examination findings.

stem: You have collected pulse-rate data of patients given a new drug being trialled as an option for supraventricular tachycardia. The data consists of the patient's initial pulse, and then a second measurement for each patient 5 minutes after being given the drug. Initial analysis of the data-set reveals that the differences between the two measurements do not follow a normal distribution. Which of the following statistical tests would be the most appropriate to use to determine whether there was a significant difference between the pulse rate before and after the provision of the new drug?
explanation:
Wilcoxon signed-rank test
Wilcoxon signed-rank test is the most appropriate test to use in this situation. As the data is paired but not normally distributed, nonparametric measures should be used in the analysis process (exceptions can sometimes be made if the sample size is extremely large and the distribution only slightly skewed). Wilcoxon signed-rank test is the non-parametric test used when data is in the form of two paired measurements (e.g., 2 pulse measurements for the same patient in this case). It does not assume a normal distribution but does assume that the data is symmetrical. The test ranks the differences between the values and then calculates whether the values are likely to come from the same population (i.e., whether there is a true difference between the before and after measurements).

Paired sample t-test
Paired sample t-test is incorrect; this is used for paired data as in this case, but one of the key assumptions for justifying the use of this test is that the data is normally distributed. This is not the case in this scenario.

Mann-Whitney U test
Mann-Whitney U test is incorrect; whilst this is used for non-parametric data as in this scenario, it is not used for paired data.

One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA)
One-way ANOVA is incorrect; this is used to compare the means of parametric data when there are more than 2 groups.

Independent sample t-test
Independent sample t-test is incorrect; this is used for parametric, nonpaired data.

stem: A gastroenterologist is writing a meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials into the comparative efficacy of octreotide and terlipressin at reducing morbidity associated with upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage. What might they wish to include to highlight any potential publication bias in their analysis?
explanation:
Funnel plot
Funnel plots are scatter plots which plot treatment effect size estimated from individual studies (x-axis) against the study size (y-axis). In an unbiased meta-analysis, results from small studies will scatter widely at the bottom of the graph, with the spread narrowing for larger studies. If there is bias, for example, because smaller studies showing no statistically significant effects go unpublished, this leads to an asymmetrical appearance of the funnel plot.

Blobbogram
Blobbograms are used to display the results of all the constituent studies included in a meta-analysis. Conventionally, each study is represented with a data point showing the odds ratio (e.g. of death in placebo vs control) with error bars representing a 95% confidence interval. They do not provide any information on publication bias in terms of which studies were included in a meta-analysis.

Box plot
Box plots are used for the visual representation of quantitative results. They are useful for showing the distribution of data points, such as the mean, range, and interquartile range of a data set, as well as the presence of positive or negative skew.

Forest plot
Forest plot is incorrect, as this is an alternative term for a blobbogram.

Histogram
Histograms are a form of bar chart which graphically represent the number of a specific type of variable that occurs within a certain range (e.g. the number of myocardial infarctions on the y-axis against patient age by decade on the x-axis).

stem: A 24-year-old man has episodic palpitations, dizziness, and occasional dyspnoea. His symptoms occur suddenly and resolve spontaneously within minutes to hours. He has no chest pain or syncope. He has no past medical or family history. During an asymptomatic period, his pulse is 80 bpm and his blood pressure is 125/74 mmHg. A cardiorespiratory examination is normal. An ECG shows an R wave with a slurred upstroke. Which ion movement is occurring most in this patient's ECG findings?
explanation:
Sodium ion influx
The presence of an R wave with a slurred upstroke on ECG suggests a delta wave, characteristic of Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome. This occurs due to an accessory pathway that conducts impulses faster than the normal conduction system through the atrioventricular (AV) node. This leads to impulses bypassing the AV node, leading to early ventricular depolarisation, resulting in a slurred upstroke in the R wave. The primary ion movement responsible for this early depolarisation is sodium ion influx through fast sodium channels during phase 0 of the action potential.

Calcium ion efflux
Calcium ion efflux is incorrect as this occurs during the repolarisation phase of the cardiac action potential. After depolarisation, calcium ions are released from the cardiomyocyte sarcoplasmic reticulum, entering the cytoplasm, contributing to contraction. During repolarisation, calcium ions leave cells, allowing them to return to their resting membrane potential. Calcium efflux could be considered in scenarios where there is disruption in normal cardiac repolarisation or in specific arrhythmias that involve prolonged action potentials, such as long QT syndrome. In these cases, abnormal calcium handling can lead to delayed repolarisation and increased risk of arrhythmias.

Potassium ion efflux
Potassium ion efflux is incorrect. Potassium efflux occurs during repolarisation, not during the early ventricular depolarisation seen in WPW. The delta wave results from sodium influx through an accessory pathway, not potassium dynamics. Potassium efflux is significant in conditions like hyperkalaemia, which causes peaked T waves and QRS widening, or hypokalaemia, which leads to U waves and increased arrhythmia risk.

Potassium ion influx
Potassium ion influx is incorrect. Potassium influx is negligible in depolarisation. Instead, potassium efflux is essential for repolarisation and maintaining normal cardiac rhythm. Potassium influx occurs during funny currents (If) in pacemaker cells. This involves sodium and potassium ion influx for diastolic depolarisation, which controls the spontaneous electrical activity of sinoatrial myocytes and the heart rate. Conditions where potassium influx is relevant include certain cardiac channelopathies, where abnormal potassium handling affects excitability, but these typically present with different ECG findings.

Sodium ion efflux
Sodium ion efflux is incorrect. The delta wave results from depolarisation, characterised by sodium entering, not leaving, the cell. Sodium efflux occurs during later repolarisation phases, not during early ventricular depolarisation. Sodium efflux plays a role in conditions like myocardial ischaemia, where altered sodium handling can lead to arrhythmias or cellular injury, but this does not apply to WPW.

stem: A 74-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a fall onto an outstretched arm. He has a past medical history of osteoporosis and his medications include calcium and vitamin D and alendronic acid. On examination, he is tender at the proximal humerus and is unable to abduct his shoulder. Examination of the elbow, wrist and hand is unremarkable. Plain radiography demonstrates a fracture of the proximal humerus. What nerve has been injured?
explanation:
Axillary nerve
Shoulder abduction - deltoid muscle - axillary nerve (C5,C6). The axillary nerve is the correct answer. This elderly man with osteoporosis has sustained a fall onto an outstretched hand resulting in a proximal humerus fracture. Fractures of this type are associated with axillary nerve injury. Injury to this nerve results in loss of the ability to abduct the shoulder due to denervation of the deltoid muscle.

Long thoracic nerve
The long thoracic nerve is incorrect. Injury to this nerve is typically caused by injuries to the ribs. It causes 'winging' of the scapula. The term 'winged scapula' is used when the muscles of the scapula are weak or paralysed, resulting in limited ability to stabilise the scapula. As a result, the medial border of the scapula protrudes, like wings. This is not an abnormality in this case. Additionally, the mechanism of injury and examination findings suggest a humeral fracture rather than a rib injury.

Musculocutaneous nerve
The musculocutaneous nerve is incorrect. Injury to this nerve causes an inability to flex the elbow. It is rarely an isolated injury and more commonly is caused by injury to the brachial plexus. Given the examination finding is an inability to abduct the shoulder rather than flex the elbow, this is less likely.

Radial nerve
The radial nerve is incorrect. Injury to this nerve is often caused by a midshaft fracture of the humerus. It will result in a 'wrist drop', which is an inability to dorsiflex the wrist. This is therefore not the likely nerve that has been injured.

Ulnar nerve
The ulnar nerve is incorrect. A possible mechanism of injury to this nerve is a fracture of the medial epicondyle. The resulting deformity will be a 'claw hand', which is when the fourth and fifth digits are flexed and the patient cannot straighten these two fingers. This is not the case here and this is, therefore, less likely.

stem: A 47-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a several-day history of productive green cough and fever. Pneumonia is suspected and so a chest X-ray is performed, which demonstrates right lower zone consolidation. In addition to this, however, multiple lesions suggestive of granulomas are noted on the X-ray. The patient explains that, many years ago, he contracted tuberculosis (TB) and that the granulomas are known. Which cytokine is responsible for activating the cells that primarily form these structures?
explanation:
Interferon-γ (IFN-γ)
Interferon-γ is responsible for activating macrophages. The cells that are being referred to here are macrophages, which are the primary constituents of granulomatous structures in diseases such as tuberculosis. Classically, macrophages are activated by Interferon-γ and so this is the correct answer.

Tumour necrosis factor-α (TNF-α)
TNF-α is secreted by macrophages and plays a wide variety of roles in the immune system, including the induction of fever and, to a lesser extent, also activating further macrophages.

Interleukin-6 (IL-6)
Interleukin-6 is incorrect - this is secreted by macrophages and Th2 cells but is not known to be a key player in the activation of macrophages. One of its main functions includes the stimulation of differentiation of B cells.

Interleukin-8 (IL-8)
Interleukin-8 is incorrect - this is secreted by macrophages and is known to act as a chemotactic agent for neutrophils, attracting them to a site of inflammation/infection.

Interleukin-10 (IL-10)
Interleukin-10 is incorrect. This is secreted by Th2 cells and seems to act in a negative-feedback manner, inhibiting the expression of further cytokines and inhibiting the expression of co-stimulatory molecules on macrophages.

stem: A 55-year-old man is referred to the outpatient cardiology clinic with fatigue and weight gain. He has had type II diabetes for 15 years, with borderline glycaemic control using metformin. An echocardiogram was performed, which showed a globally dilated left ventricle with a reduced ejection fraction, estimated at 30%. NT-proBNP was 1256 (<125 pg/mL). A decision is made to start empagliflozin, due to its cardioprotective value in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. What is the primary site of action for this new medication?
explanation:
Proximal convoluted tubule
The majority of glucose reabsorption in the nephron occurs within the proximal convoluted tubule. Sodium-glucose cotransporter (SGLT2) proteins are responsible for the resorption of approximately 90% of filtered glucose. Inhibition results in glycosuria and natriuresis as the protein is a cotransporter. SGLT2-inhibitors have been shown to significantly reduce the risk of hospitalisation in patients with heart failure. Interestingly, even though the glucose-lowering efficacy of SGLT2-inhibitors declines at lower eGFR rates, the cardiovascular benefits are preserved.

Ascending loop of Henle
Ascending loop of Henle is not correct. Loop diuretics predominantly act at the apical membrane in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, inhibiting the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter.

Collecting duct
Collecting duct is not correct. Aldosterone receptor antagonists exert their diuretic effects within the collecting duct and distal convoluted tubule.

Descending loop of Henle
Descending loop of Henle is not correct. The descending limb is largely impermeable to ions and highly permeable to water. It contributes to generating the counter-current multiplication system and is responsible for most of the nephron's water-resorbing capacity.

Distal convoluted tubule
Distal convoluted tubule is not correct. Thiazide diuretics act on the sodium-chloride transporter in the distal convoluted tubule (DCT). There are SGLT1 proteins contained within the DCT, but these are unaffected by SGLT2 inhibitors.

stem: A study is performed comparing two chemotherapy regimes for patients with small cell lung cancer. The end point of the study is survival time. Which one of the following types statistical measures is it most appropriate to compare survival time with?
explanation:
Hazard ratio
The hazard ratio is typically used when analysing survival over time. The most appropriate statistical measure to compare survival time in this study is the hazard ratio. Hazard ratio is a measure of the rate at which events (in this case, death) occur in one group compared to another group over time. It takes into account both the number of events and the time at which they occur, making it suitable for comparing survival times between different treatment groups.

Odds ratio
Odds ratio is not the best choice here because it measures the odds of an event occurring in one group compared to another group. While it can be used to compare binary outcomes (such as presence or absence of disease), it does not take into account the timing of events, which is crucial when comparing survival times.

Pearson's product-moment coefficient
Pearson's product-moment coefficient measures the linear correlation between two continuous variables. It would not be appropriate for comparing survival times between treatment groups, as it does not provide information on how much better one treatment is than another in terms of prolonging survival.

Relative risk
Relative risk, also known as risk ratio, compares the probability of an event occurring in one group versus another group. Although relative risk can be used to compare binary outcomes like hazard ratio, it does not take into account the timing of events. This makes the hazard ratio a more suitable choice for comparing survival times.

Absolute risk reduction
Finally, absolute risk reduction measures the difference in risk between two groups. While it can provide useful information about treatment efficacy, it also does not consider the timing of events and therefore is less suited for comparing survival times.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents to her GP with an 8-month history of fatigue and diarrhoea and a recent onset of an itchy, vesicular rash on both elbows and buttocks. She denies passing any blood per rectum and has had no recent exposure to chickenpox or shingles. Blood tests show the following: Hb 9.6 g/L Male: (135-180) Female: (115 - 160) MCV 78fL (80 - 100) MCH 26pg (28-33) RDW 14% (11-15) Platelets 221 * 109/L (150 - 400) WBC 6.7 * 109/L (4.0 - 11.0) In addition to auto-antibodies, HLA typing is sent and further investigations including skin biopsy of the affected areas are arranged. What human leucocyte antigen (HLA) subtypes is this patient's skin condition most commonly associated with?
explanation:
HLA-DR3
Dermatitis herpetiformis is associated with HLA-DR3. It is a skin condition that is regarded as a cutaneous manifestation of coeliac disease. This patient has presented with a long history of fatigue and diarrhoea with a probable iron deficiency anaemia, which is consistent with a diagnosis of coeliac disease. Dermatitis herpetiformis commonly affects the forearms, legs and buttocks and is typically an itchy vesicular rash that resembles herpes virus infection.

HLA-B27
HLA-B27 is associated with a range of diseases including ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, and ulcerative colitis. It is not, however, typically associated with dermatitis herpetiformis.

HLA-B51
Behcet's disease is most commonly associated with HLA-B51.

HLA-DQ8
While coeliac disease is associated with HLA-DQ2 and DQ8, it is the HLA-DR3 subtype that is most commonly associated with dermatitis herpetiformis.

HLA-DR4
Type 1 diabetes mellitus is typically associated with HLA-DR4. It may also be associated with HLA-DR3.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a nosebleed that has been ongoing for 2 hours despite applying pressure. She reports having had three similar episodes in the past 6 months. She also mentions easy bruising and prolonged bleeding after dental extraction last month. She takes no regular medications and has no significant past medical history. On examination, she has multiple ecchymoses on her limbs of varying ages. Her vital signs are stable. Blood tests are performed. Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-160) Platelets 245 × 10^9/L (150-400) White cell count 7.2 × 10^9/L (4.0-11.0) Prothrombin time (PT) 19.2 seconds (11.5-15.5) Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) 32 seconds (30-40) Thrombin time (TT) 14 seconds (14-16) Fibrinogen 2.8 g/L (2.0-4.0) What is the most likely bleeding disorder?
explanation:
Factor VII deficiency
Factor VII deficiency is the most likely diagnosis in this case. The patient has a prolonged prothrombin time (PT) with normal activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) and thrombin time (TT). Factor VII is a crucial component of the extrinsic coagulation pathway, which is measured by the PT. When Factor VII is deficient, the PT is prolonged while the aPTT, which measures the intrinsic and common pathways, remains normal. This isolated prolongation of PT with normal aPTT is characteristic of Factor VII deficiency. Factor VII deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive bleeding disorder with an estimated prevalence of 1 in 500,000. The clinical presentation typically includes mucocutaneous bleeding such as epistaxis (nosebleeds), easy bruising, and menorrhagia in women, which aligns with this patient's presentation. The severity of bleeding can vary widely, from mild to severe, depending on the degree of factor deficiency.

von Willebrand disease
Von Willebrand disease is incorrect in this scenario. While it is the most common inherited bleeding disorder and can present with mucocutaneous bleeding similar to our patient, the laboratory findings would be different. Von Willebrand disease typically presents with a normal or slightly prolonged PT, potentially prolonged aPTT (especially in type 2N and 3), and reduced von Willebrand factor antigen and activity levels. The isolated prolongation of PT with normal aPTT seen in this patient is not consistent with von Willebrand disease.

Factor VIII deficiency
Factor VIII deficiency (Haemophilia A) is not the correct diagnosis here. Haemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder that primarily affects males, though female carriers can occasionally be symptomatic. More importantly, Factor VIII is part of the intrinsic pathway, so its deficiency would lead to a prolonged aPTT with a normal PT. Our patient has the opposite pattern with a prolonged PT and normal aPTT, ruling out Factor VIII deficiency.

Factor IX deficiency
Factor IX deficiency (Haemophilia B) is also incorrect. Like Haemophilia A, it is an X-linked recessive disorder affecting the intrinsic pathway. A deficiency in Factor IX would result in a prolonged aPTT with a normal PT, which does not match our patient's coagulation profile showing a prolonged PT with normal aPTT.

Vitamin K deficiency
Vitamin K deficiency is not the most likely diagnosis in this case. While vitamin K deficiency can cause a prolonged PT due to reduced synthesis of vitamin K-dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X), it typically affects multiple coagulation factors simultaneously. This usually results in prolongation of both PT and aPTT, especially in more severe deficiency states. Additionally, our patient has no risk factors mentioned for vitamin K deficiency such as malnutrition, malabsorption, antibiotic use, or liver disease. The isolated PT prolongation with completely normal aPTT is more suggestive of an isolated Factor VII deficiency rather than vitamin K deficiency.

stem: Which one of the following is the most common genetic cause of Prader-Willi syndrome?
explanation:
Microdeletion of the paternal 15q11-13
Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) is a genetic disorder that results from the loss of function of specific genes in a particular region of chromosome 15 (15q11-q13). The genes are maternally imprinted and paternally expressed, which means they are normally silenced on the maternal chromosome and only active on the paternal chromosome. Thus, when there is a microdeletion on the paternal chromosome in this region, it leads to PWS as these genes are not expressed. This accounts for approximately 70% of cases.

Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15
Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15 is also a cause of Prader-Willi syndrome but it is less common than microdeletion. In this case, both copies of chromosome 15 are inherited from the mother rather than one from each parent. As mentioned earlier, the relevant genes in PWS are silenced on the maternal chromosome so if both chromosomes are maternally derived, then there will be no active copy of these genes leading to PWS.

Paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15
Paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15 does not cause Prader-Willi syndrome because having two active copies of these genes would not lead to loss-of-function which characterises PWS. Instead, it can result in Angelman syndrome if there's a mutation or deletion in the region where UBE3A gene is located since it's only expressed from the maternal allele.

Microdeletion of the maternal 15q11-13
Microdeletion of the maternal 15q11-13, like paternal uniparental disomy, does not cause Prader-Willi syndrome because these genes are typically inactive on the maternal side anyway. However, this can lead to Angelman Syndrome due to loss-of-function mutation or deletion at UBE3A gene which is usually only expressed from this allele.

Trisomy 18
Trisomy 18, also known as Edwards Syndrome, has no relation to Prader-Willi syndrome. It occurs when there's an extra copy (total of three copies) of all or part of chromosome 18 and it causes severe intellectual disability and physical abnormalities including heart defects.

stem: Which one of the following best describes the main action of the polymerase chain reaction?
explanation:
DNA amplification
The correct answer is DNA amplification. The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is primarily used to amplify a specific region of DNA, producing millions or billions of copies. This process involves several steps: denaturation, annealing and elongation. In the denaturation step, the double-stranded DNA is heated to separate it into two single strands. During the annealing step, primers bind to each original strand on opposite ends of the sequence to be amplified. In the elongation phase, a heat-stable DNA polymerase synthesises new strands of DNA starting from the primers.

DNA identification using RNA
DNA identification using RNA is not correct as PCR does not involve RNA for identifying DNA. While there are techniques that utilise RNA, such as reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR), where RNA is first converted into complementary DNA (cDNA) before amplification, this is not the primary action of PCR itself.

RNA translation to protein
The option RNA translation to protein refers to a completely different biological process that occurs in cells where messenger RNA (mRNA) code is used by ribosomes to assemble amino acids into proteins. This process does not involve PCR.

RNA amplification
RNA amplification can be achieved through a method known as RT-PCR as mentioned earlier but again this isn't what happens in basic PCR. Instead, it's an extension of the technique which allows for amplification and detection of RNA sequences.

DNA to RNA conversion
DNA to RNA conversion, also known as transcription, takes place in cells where segments of DNA are used as templates to create corresponding RNA molecules. This process also doesn't involve PCR and therefore this option isn't correct either.

stem: A 31-year-old woman with a history of severe allergic asthma is reviewed in a specialist asthma clinic. She describes poor control with frequent use of short-acting beta-agonists, despite being on optimised standard therapy. She has previously completed multiple full trials of oral corticosteroids in the past year. Consequently, she is considered for further treatment with monoclonal antibodies. What cells produce the target of these antibodies?
explanation:
Plasma cells
Plasma cells are responsible for producing IgE. After IgE is released, it binds to the Fc domain on the IgE receptor found on mast cells and basophils. In response to an allergen, this receptor-bound IgE causes degranulation and release of allergic mediators including histamine that form the allergy cascade. Omalizumab is a monoclonal antibody that selectively binds to the domain at which IgE normally does, preventing interaction with its receptor.

Basophils
Basophils secrete IL-4 and histamine.

Dendritic cells
Dendritic cells secrete pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-a and IL-12. They respond to foreign allergens by activating Th2 cells and indirectly contribute to IgE production.

Mast cells
Mast cells secrete leukotrienes, prostaglandins and histamine.

Natural killer cells
Natural killer cells secrete TNF-α, IL-10 and IFN-Î³.

stem: A rheumatology registrar reviews a patient in clinic with non-specific lower back pain. He occasionally finds it frustrating to deal with this problem as it can be difficult to manage and seeks to find an intervention that might help this patient cohort and sets about investigating possibilities for treatment. He wonders whether turmeric might be of benefit. He designs a study to assess whether this treatment is of benefit. The patients are asked to rate their back pain on a scale of 1-10 prior to treatment, where 1 is none and 10 is very severe. They are then given treatment with turmeric for two weeks and reassessed with the same back pain rating scale. Given the data is not normally distributed, what statistical test is appropriate to determine if there is a statistically significant difference in back pain with treatment?
explanation:
Wilcoxon signed-rank test
Wilcoxon signed-rank test: This is the correct answer. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is a non-parametric test used to compare paired samples when the data is not normally distributed. It is suitable for determining whether there is a statistically significant difference in the median scores of the back pain ratings before and after the turmeric treatment in the same group of patients.

Chi-squared test
Chi-squared test: This test is used to examine the association between categorical variables and is not appropriate for comparing continuous data, such as back pain scores, especially when the data is paired and non-normally distributed.

Mann Whitney U Test
Mann Whitney U Test: This is another non-parametric test, but it is used to compare differences between two independent groups rather than paired data. Since the study involves paired measurements (the same patients before and after treatment), the Mann Whitney U Test would not be suitable.

Student's t-test (paired)
Student's t-test (paired): The paired t-test is used to compare means of two related groups. However, it assumes that the data is normally distributed. Since the data in this case is not normally distributed, the paired t-test is not appropriate.

Student's t-test (unpaired)
Student's t-test (unpaired): The unpaired t-test (also known as an independent t-test) is used to compare the means of two independent groups, not paired data. Additionally, like the paired t-test, it assumes normal distribution, making it unsuitable for this scenario.

stem: A 32-year-old woman is referred to the oncology clinic after being diagnosed with breast cancer. Her mother died of breast cancer at age 35, and her brother was diagnosed with osteosarcoma at age 18. Her maternal aunt had leukaemia at age 28. Genetic testing reveals a germline mutation in the TP53 gene. What is the primary cellular function affected by this mutation?
explanation:
Cell cycle checkpoint regulation
p53 - plays a crucial role in the cell cycle, preventing entry into the S phase until DNA has been checked and repaired. Cell cycle checkpoint regulation is the primary cellular function affected by the TP53 gene mutation in this patient with Li-Fraumeni syndrome. p53 (the protein encoded by TP53) acts as a crucial checkpoint regulator that prevents cells with damaged DNA from progressing through the cell cycle. Specifically, p53 can halt progression at the G1/S checkpoint, allowing time for DNA repair before DNA replication occurs in S phase. When DNA damage is detected, p53 is activated and initiates transcription of genes involved in cell cycle arrest, DNA repair, or apoptosis if the damage is irreparable. In Li-Fraumeni syndrome, germline mutations in TP53 compromise this checkpoint function, allowing cells with damaged DNA to replicate, which significantly increases cancer risk across multiple tissue types. The family history in this case is classic for Li-Fraumeni syndrome, with early-onset breast cancer, osteosarcoma, and leukaemia across multiple family members.

DNA damage repair
DNA damage repair is closely related to p53 function but is not its primary role. While p53 can upregulate genes involved in DNA repair pathways in response to damage, it does not directly repair DNA itself. Rather, it coordinates the cellular response to DNA damage by activating repair mechanisms, arresting the cell cycle, or triggering apoptosis. The primary function of p53 is as a transcription factor that regulates these processes, with cell cycle checkpoint control being its most critical function.

Mitochondrial energy production
Mitochondrial energy production is not a primary function of p53. Although p53 has been shown to influence mitochondrial metabolism and can translocate to mitochondria during apoptosis, its main role is not related to energy production. The cancer predisposition in Li-Fraumeni syndrome results from defective cell cycle control rather than metabolic dysfunction.

Protein synthesis inhibition
Protein synthesis inhibition is not a primary function of p53. While p53 can affect protein synthesis indirectly through its transcriptional activity, it does not directly inhibit protein synthesis machinery. p53 primarily functions as a transcription factor that regulates the expression of target genes involved in cell cycle arrest, DNA repair, and apoptosis.

Cellular membrane integrity
Cellular membrane integrity is not a primary function of p53. p53 does not play a significant role in maintaining membrane structure or function. The increased cancer susceptibility in Li-Fraumeni syndrome is due to defective cell cycle regulation and inability to eliminate cells with DNA damage, not membrane abnormalities.

stem: Which one of the following causes of primary immunodeficiency is a T-cell disorder?
explanation:
DiGeorge syndrome
DiGeorge syndrome is a primary immunodeficiency disorder caused by T-cell deficiency and dysfunction. It is an example of a microdeletion syndrome. Patients are consequently at increased risk of viral and fungal infections.

stem: A 1-day-old baby has been found to have a cleft palate and facial dysmorphia during the newborn infant physical examination. He is also observed to have some respiratory difficulties during feeding, and echocardiography has revealed an interrupted aortic arch. Subsequent blood tests have also shown hypocalcemia. His parents have been informed of the likely diagnosis and the implications, including the propensity for recurrent infections during childhood. What underlying immunodeficiency is responsible for this?
explanation:
T cell deficiency
DiGeorge syndrome - a T-cell disorder This baby most likely has DiGeorge syndrome, which is also known as 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. This is associated with congenital heart defects, abnormal facies (including cleft lip and/or palate), congenital absence of the thymus gland and hypocalcemia. The mnemonic CATCH22 (cardiac abnormality, abnormal facies, thymic aplasia, cleft palate, hypocalcemia, chromosome 22) is commonly used to remember these clinical features. DiGeorge syndrome is a primary immunodeficiency characterised by T-cell deficiency as the thymus is critical in the development of the T-cell immune system. This manifests in severe and sometimes unusual viral and fungal infections in early infancy, such as bronchiolitis, diarrhoea, oral candidiasis and Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia.

B cell deficiency
B cell deficiency is incorrect. An example of this disorder is a common variable immune deficiency (CVID), which is associated with a high risk of autoimmune disorders and malignancy, as well as severe bacterial infections.

Defective complement system
Defective complement system is incorrect. Conditions associated with this defect include mannose-binding lectin (MBL) deficiency, which is associated with recurrent bacterial infections.

Defective neutrophils
Defective neutrophils is an incorrect option. An example of this defect is chronic granulomatous disease arising from certain X-linked recessive disorders.

Leucocyte function defect
Leucocyte function defect is incorrect. An example of this defect is leucocyte adhesion deficiency, which leads to the inability of neutrophils to migrate to sites of infection and can result in delayed wound healing and deep-seated skin infections.
